house:119:1:145.short_description: H.R.1 House reconciliation package: selected border, detention and asylum, employment-authorization and selected sponsor/enforcement fees
house:119:1:145.compact_description: Selected House H.R. 1 provisions would fund border infrastructure and detention, set fiscal 2025 asylum filing/pending fee floors of $1,000/$100 and specified asylum/parole/TPS employment-authorization initial/renewal fee floors of $550, and limit those documents to at most six months. This is a whole-package passage choice, with qualifications.
house:119:1:145.meaning:
This May22 House passage is the whole H.R.1 reconciliation package, not a separate immigration-only vote. The controlling House choice uses H.Res.436: Rules Committee Print119-3 modified by the amendment printed in H.Rept.119-113 was considered adopted. The retained Immigration clauses are reconstructed against that chain and the contemporaneous as-amended floor Record. The currently served EH incorporates later corrections and renumbering and is a comparison witness for these unchanged selected clauses, not the controlling entire vote-time text. Later engrossment corrections and the July Senate replacement are not silently substituted for this choice. The description selects border infrastructure, detention, State reimbursement and asylum-fee mechanisms; it does not inventory every immigration-related tax, benefit, employment-authorization, child-sponsor or removal provision in this multi-domain package. Section60001 would make additional fiscal2025 CBP appropriations available until September30,2029: $46.5billion for primary/waterborne/secondary barriers, access roads and associated detection attributes; a separate $50million for specified invasive plants impeding RioGrande border operations; and $5billion for CBP facilities/checkpoints near the southwest, northern and maritime borders. These are different purposes, not one immigration-enforcement account or actual expenditures. The adopted manager amendment adds section60004: $12billion in additional fiscal2025 DHS funds, available until September30,2029, for grants reimbursing States for costs of actions on or after January21,2021 assisting federal border/immigration enforcement, including detention/removal and combating unlawful entry of persons/contraband. Applications need satisfactory cost evidence, and DHS cannot reimburse a State already reimbursed under another DHS grant program. This is funding subject to a process and conditions, not proof of State awards or a newly conferred State removal power. Section70101 would appropriate an additional $45billion for fiscal2025 to ICE, available until September30,2029, solely for single-adult alien detention and family residential-center capacity. DHS MAY detain family units pending a removal decision and, if ordered removed, until removal. Its family-center definition includes accompanied alien children, excludes unaccompanied alien children, and expressly applies regardless of State/local facility licensing. Its single-adult detention standards clause says they shall be set in the Secretary's SOLE discretion. Preserve that printed language without importing the Senate's express consistent-with-applicable-law qualification or deciding its interaction with judicial/other legal constraints. The existing unaccompanied-child definition in6USC279(g)(2) requires no lawful immigration status, age under18, and no US parent/legal guardian or none available for care/physical custody; childhood alone does not establish that category. Capacity funding and permission are not a universal detention mandate, removal order or actual detention outcome. Section70002 would require an additional fee at the time an alien files an asylum application: the fiscal2025 amount may be set by rule but cannot be less than $1,000. It cannot be waived/reduced. From fiscal2026 its amount increases using the prior fiscal-year fee and the printed July-to-July CPI-U increase, with the increment rounded down to a multiple of $10. Half of the Attorney-General-filed receipts go to EOIR; half of DHS-filed receipts go to USCIS's existing Immigration Examinations Fee Account; those credited amounts may be retained/spent without further appropriation, and the remainder goes to Treasury. Section70010 separately requires a fee for EACH CALENDAR YEAR an application remains pending, initially at least $100 for fiscal2025, with later CPI-U adjustment, Treasury disposition and no waiver/reduction. Its printed adjustment has no express rounding term; the filing-fee rounding rule is not copied into it. These are separate filing and pending-application charges, not fixed lifetime amounts or a claim that every asylum applicant actually paid. Section70023 changes existing INA208(d)(3)/8USC1158(d)(3) from MAY impose fees to SHALL, strikes the following cost-cap/installment/nonmandatory-fee language and preserves authority to set additional adjudication/naturalization fees under286(m). The existing paragraph already allowed fees for asylum consideration, employment authorization and asylum-based adjustment and capped them at adjudication costs; the bill does not create first-ever fee authority or establish a new substantive asylum eligibility test through that edit. Existing1356(m)/(n) supply the account/cost-recovery context. Employment-authorization provisions are separate from asylum filing and annual pending-application fees. House70003 would charge an additional fee on initial employment-authorization applications for asylum applicants underINA208(d)(2), paroled aliens and applicants underTPS244(a)(1)(B). Each initial fee has a fiscal2025 floor of$550, may be higher by DHS rule, cannot be waived/reduced and has the printed fiscal2026-onward July-to-July CPI-U increment rounded down to$10. All three initial authorizations would last no more than six months. In70003(a)(4), the House allocation sentence says25percent of fees received UNDER THIS SECTION goes to USCIS's existing fee account to retain/spend without further appropriation, with50percent of that credited amount for benefit-fraud detection/prevention; uncredited amounts go to Treasury. The separately printed parole/TPS subsections direct their fees to Treasury. Preserve those exact scope words rather than silently deciding their interaction. House70012 and70014 separately impose additional parole/TPS employment-authorization renewal or extension fees with fiscal2025$550floors, possible higher rule amounts, subsequent CPI increments rounded down to$10, Treasury disposition and no waiver/reduction. Both initial and renewed/extended authorizations in those sections last no more than six months. House70013 imposes at least$550 for each asylum-based renewal/extension, Treasury disposition and no waiver/reduction; that section prints no annual inflation formula. DHS MAY provide asylum-applicant employment authorization for at most six months, and each renewal/extension also has that limit. Authorization terminates immediately after an asylum-officer denial unless referred to an immigration judge;30days after an immigration-judge denial unless timely appealed to BIA; or immediately after BIA denies an appeal of asylum denial. After such termination DHS cannot grant, renew or extend it unless a FederalCourtOfAppeals remands to BIA. This restriction concerns employment authorization, not an automatic asylum denial, immediate removal or a bar on all judicial review. The pre-vote1158(d)(2) already says asylum applicants are not entitled to employment authorization but it may be provided by regulation; applicants not otherwise eligible cannot receive it before180days after asylum filing. Existing1254a(a)(1)(B)/(a)(2) authorizes employment and makes work authorization effective throughout TPS. Fee/document-validity provisions do not themselves end TPS, create first work authority or establish everyone's eligibility. The existing parole paragraph1182(d)(5)(A)/(B) is case-by-case urgent-humanitarian/significant-public-benefit authority subject to the printed statutory exceptions, including the refugee qualification and does not constitute admission. These fees do not supply a grant of parole or automatic employment permission. House70007 imposes a separate additional sponsor-placement fee, collected by HHS from the individual BEFORE placing an unaccompanied alien child underTVPRA235(c). Its fiscal2025 floor is$3,500 or a higher rule amount, with fiscal2026-onward July-to-July CPI-U increments rounded down to$10 and no waiver/reduction. The stated purpose is partial reimbursement for the child's prior federal-custody processing, housing, food, education, transport and other care.25percent goes to HHS to retain/spend without further appropriation for sponsor/adult-household background checks; the remainder goes to Treasury. The specified checks include names, SSNs, dates of birth, validated residence, immigration status and contact information for the sponsor and all adult household residents, and records checks including sex-offender registry, public-records background and fingerprint-based national criminal history. Existing1232(c) already requires protective/suitability assessments, identity/relationship verification, independent risk findings and home studies in specified cases. This is not first-ever sponsor vetting or a new assertion that any sponsor has criminal activity. House70020 imposes ANOTHER additional sponsor fee BEFORE the unaccompanied child's release to the sponsor. Its fiscal2025 floor is$5,000 or a higher rule amount with later CPI increments rounded down to$10, Treasury disposition and no waiver/reduction. Despite its failure-to-appear title, collection is not conditioned on a child already missing court or having an in-absentia order. At the end of the child's immigration proceedings as an unaccompanied child OR at the end of that sponsorship, HHS MAY reimburse if the sponsor demonstrates the child was not ordered removed in absentia. If such an order was rescinded underINA240(b)(5)(C), the sponsor MAY SEEK reimbursement. Neither reimbursement pathway is an automatic refund. The two sponsor fees remain distinct additional charges; there is no claim that every applicant actually paid them or that payment establishes suitability. Existing1232(c) placement protections and279(g)(2) UAC definition remain material context; their interaction with fee collection is not a finding of actual placement, detention or legal enforceability. House70021 requires a separate fiscal2025 fee of at least$5,000, possibly higher by rule, on an alien BOTH ordered removed in absentia under1229a(b)(5) AND subsequently arrested by ICE. It has later CPI increments rounded down to$10, Treasury disposition and no waiver/reduction, and does not apply if the underlying order was rescinded under1229a(b)(5)(C). House70022 separately charges any INADMISSIBLE alien at the time CBP apprehends the person BETWEEN PORTS OF ENTRY; its fiscal2025 floor is$5,000 or higher by rule, later CPI increments rounded down to$10, Treasury disposition and no waiver/reduction. Do not treat every arrest, port-of-entry encounter, unadmitted person or failure to attend court as satisfying these exact fee predicates. The complete pre-vote1229a(b)(5) and(e) retain the written-notice rule and failure-to-provide-address exception, clear/unequivocal/convincing evidence of notice and removability, and separate rescission routes: a motion within180days showing exceptional circumstances beyond the alien's control, or at any time for missing statutory notice or no-fault failure while in federal/state custody. Filing those motions stays removal pending the immigration judge's disposition. Exceptional circumstances include the specified battery/extreme cruelty or serious illness/death examples, excluding less compelling circumstances; removability distinguishes inadmissibility for an unadmitted alien from deportability for an admitted alien.1229(a) preserves notice/address/change-of-hearing context. The fee provisions do not themselves create an in-absentia order, repeal rescission, establish a new removal ground or prove an individual enforcement outcome. House70004 adds a parole-entry fee with fiscal2025floor$1,000 or a higher DHS rule amount, fiscal2026-onward July-to-July CPI-U increments rounded down to$10, Treasury disposition and no waiver/reduction for an applicable fee. It applies to each alien paroled into the US EXCEPT where the alien establishes one of the printed parole-reason exceptions; fee exceptions are not erased by the separate waiver bar. The fee exceptions retain their actual predicates: a medical emergency with necessary treatment unavailable in the foreign state where the alien resides OR a life-threatening emergency with insufficient normal-visa time; the parent/legal guardian of such a medical-emergency MINOR; the alien needed in the US to donate an organ or tissue for transplant, with insufficient normal-visa time; a close family member in the United States whose death is imminent, when normal visa processing would prevent arriving while that person is alive; or seeking to attend a close family member's funeral, when normal visa processing would prevent arriving in the United States in time for it; an adopted child's urgent treatment needed before expected final adoption-related visa issuance while in the petitioner's legal custody; a LAWFUL INA245 adjustment applicant returning after temporary travel abroad; and a person returned to a contiguous country under235(b)(2)(C) paroled to attend the person's immigration hearing. The law-enforcement significant-public-benefit exception requires a DHS determination that significant public benefit has resulted or will result from the parole, BOTH assistance to the USGovernment AND presence required in that matter, PLUS at least one of inadmissibility, failure to meet nonimmigrant-admission eligibility, or insufficient normal-visa time; it is not every asserted public benefit. House exception9 separately requires a Cuban national LIVING IN CUBA, an approvedINA203(a) petition, no immediately available immigrant visa, all immigrant-visa eligibility requirements, no other inadmissibility AND a parole grant furthering the printed US minimum-annual-legal-migration commitment under the1994/1995Cuba-USagreements. Existing1153(a) identifies family-preference visa classes; that eligibility context does not prove approval, visa availability or an actual grant. This is not an exemption for every Cuban national, every parolee or the differently printed Senate Cuban/Haitianentrant category. Existing1182(d)(5) parole authority remains subject to its printed humanitarian/public-benefit/case-by-case/statutory-exception terms and non-admission distinction; a fee or exception does not confer parole, adjustment, admission or hearing outcome. House70005 adds a separate SIJ application fee with fiscal2025floor$500 or a higher rule amount, later CPI increments rounded down to$10, Treasury disposition and no waiver/reduction. The fee predicate requires that reunification with ONEparent or legal guardian is viable despite abuse/neglect/abandonment or a similar State-law basis making reunification with the OTHERparent/legalguardian not viable. It is not stated as a fee on every SIJ applicant or an amendment creating SIJ status. Complete1101(a)(27)(J) already requires the specified USjuvenile-court dependency/custody determination and nonviable reunification with1ORboth parents on the listed State-law bases, a best-interest finding against return to the identified former country, and DHSconsent; HHS-specific custody-jurisdiction consent and no derived rights by virtue of parentage remain. Do not substitute nonimmigrantJexchange-visitor provisions, infer a UAC-under18 rule, grant status from a fee, or assume that paying changes parental rights. House70006 adds a separate TPS-consideration fee with fiscal2025floor$500 or a higher rule amount, later CPI increments rounded down to$10, Treasury disposition and no waiver/reduction. Its status predicate is an alien NOTADMITTED to the US OR an admitted NONIMMIGRANT who at TPSapplication time failed to maintain/extend the applicable nonimmigrant status (including authorized-stay compliance) OR comply with its conditions. It is not an undifferentiated fee on every TPSapplicant, an EADfee, or proof of inadmissibility/criminal conduct. The pre-vote1254a(c)(1)(B) already permits a reasonable registration fee capped$50 and a separate additional work-document fee for post-July17,1991designations, with appropriation-credit language. This House fee is ADDITIONAL to other authorized fees; the separately stated registration cap is not described as a newly created TPS application right or the House newfee's ceiling. Other TPSeligibility/work-authorization protections remain; fee liability does not establish status eligibility or an actual collection. House 70008 adds a visa-integrity fee on each alien issued a nonimmigrant visa, collected upon issuance in addition to other authorized fees. The fiscal 2025 minimum is $250 or a higher DHS rule amount; fiscal 2026 onward adds the July-to-July CPI-U increment rounded down to the next lowest multiple of $1. Unreimbursed fees go to Treasury; the applicable fee cannot be waived or reduced. DHS MAY reimburse after the visa period of validity expires if the alien demonstrates ONE of three printed alternatives: did not seek admission during that validity period; OR after admission complied with ALL visa conditions, including no unauthorized employment, AND departed no later than five days after the date authorized to remain in the US; OR FILED to extend, change or adjust status within the visa validity period. Filing is the printed third alternative, not a required grant; nonuse is its own first alternative. Reimbursement is discretionary and qualified, not an automatic refund or a new permission to stay or work. Visa validity and authorized stay are not interchangeable, and the reimbursement departure condition is not described as a general grace period. The pre-vote 1101(a)(26) definition identifies a visa properly issued to an eligible nonimmigrant by a competent officer; issuance does not itself prove admission, compliance or reimbursement. House 70009 separately adds a fee on ANY alien applying for Form I-94, with fiscal 2025 minimum $24 or a higher DHS rule amount, later July-to-July CPI-U increments, no expressly printed increment-rounding rule, and no waiver/reduction. Twenty percent of each collected application fee is deposited pursuant to existing 1356(q)(2) and available to CBP to retain and spend without further appropriation for Form I-94 processing; the remainder goes to Treasury. The existing Land Border Inspection Fee Account was already established, including I-94/I-94W/I-68 and similar land-port receipts. The new section says any alien applying for the form; the account name does not narrow that application predicate to land ports. Existing subsection (q)(3) refunds appropriations for inspection expenses, not the applicant, and is not described as a personal fee-refund entitlement. No fee amount proves an actual application, collection, admission or immigration-status outcome. House 70017 amends the existing ESTA fee, rather than creating the travel-authorization System or treating it as admission. Pre-vote 1187(h)(3) already specifies an initial fee comprising $17 per travel authorization plus an amount at least sufficient to recover full System provision/administration costs. The proposal adds a $10 MINIMUM to that cost-recovery component while retaining the full-cost condition, and adds another component of at least $13. These are components of the existing sum, not an undifferentiated $10 or $13 total fee. It limits annual deposits from the existing $17 component into the Travel Promotion Fund to not more than $20 million, sending that component's remainder to Treasury; it expressly sends the new $13 component to Treasury. The existing administration-cost component remains transferred to Treasury and available for administering the System. The sunset edit extends only the existing clause(i)(I) Travel Promotion Fund fee restriction from fiscal years beginning after October31,2028 to those beginning after October31,2034. Fiscal2026-onward CPI-U adjustment expressly names clause(i)(II), but its prior-year base literally says the amount imposed UNDER THIS SUBSECTION. The full-cost component/subsection-base relationship is preserved for application review, not silently rewritten as a CPI adjustment of an isolated $10 amount or the whole total; no increment-rounding rule is printed here. The complete pre-vote System/validity limits distinguish eligible travel from admissibility and distinguish denial of ESTA travel eligibility from denial of visa eligibility. The selected ESTA amendment prints no new express fee-waiver prohibition; none is imported from EVUS, and waiver availability is not inferred. House 70018 separately edits the existing immigration inspection/preinspection user fee in 1356(d). Its collection event remains inspection of each passenger arriving at a US port, or preinspection outside the US before arrival, aboard a COMMERCIAL aircraft or vessel. The existing $7 becomes a fiscal2025 MINIMUM of $10, with later July-to-July CPI-U increments rounded down to the next lowest $0.25 and a no-waiver/reduction clause. It expressly makes (d) subject to the retained (e) exceptions. The old non-aircraft geographical-origin exemption for Canada/Mexico/the US/adjacent islands is removed; the separate $3 commercial-vessel-origin charge is replaced with an exemption from (d) for IMMIGRATION INSPECTION AT DESIGNATED PORTS OF ENTRY of passengers arriving either by the separately defined ferry or by the specified Great Lakes vessels. A passenger in transit to an outside-US destination AND receiving no immigration inspection remains exempt. The printed ferry definition remains: a vessel outside ocean/coastwise service, providing only deck-passenger and/or vehicle capacity, a short frequent run along the most direct water route, and a public bridge/tunnel-type service. The Great Lakes branch retains its Great Lakes/connecting-waterway and regular-schedule conditions. These own predicates are not transferred between exception branches, and the fee is not described as applying to every border crossing or every inadmissible person. The new clause directs $1 per inspected/preinspected individual to Treasury; unstruck 1356(h)(1)(A) separately says ALL (d) receipts enter the Immigration User Fee Account notwithstanding other provisions. Both printed provisions and the account's appropriations-refund framework remain visible for application review, without inventing a resolved residual distribution or personal refund right. House 70019 adds an EVUS fee at enrollment for an alien SUBJECT to that System, in addition to other authorized fees. Fiscal2025 minimum is $30 or a higher DHS rule amount; later CPI-U increments round down to $0.25 and the fee cannot be waived or reduced. It establishes a separate CBP EVUS Account; fees enter that account LESS $5 PER ENROLLMENT directed to Treasury. Account deposits are appropriated without further appropriation and available until expended for CBP costs administering EVUS. The collection event, quarter-dollar increment and fixed Treasury deduction are distinct from ESTA or the commercial-passenger inspection fee; no new System eligibility, admission, visa grant, compliance determination or actual collection follows from the fee. House 70011 adds a fee for EACH continuance that an alien BOTH REQUESTS and IS GRANTED by an immigration judge. The fiscal2025 minimum is $100 or a higher AttorneyGeneral rule amount, with fiscal2026-onward July-to-July CPI-U increments and no expressly printed increment-rounding rule. Fees go to Treasury. The no-waiver/reduction clause preserves a separate NO-FEE exception when the requested continuance is granted BASED ON the defined exceptional circumstances. Complete pre-vote1229a(e)(1), the section240 definition, requires circumstances BEYOND THE ALIEN'S CONTROL and excludes less compelling circumstances. Its examples are illustrative, not an exclusive list: battery/extreme cruelty to the alien or the alien's child/parent; serious illness of the alien; or serious illness/death of the alien's spouse/child/parent. Those own person/event predicates are not collapsed into any family illness/death, and ordinary good cause or a continuance request alone is not described as satisfying the statutory fee exception. The proposal does not charge a denied request merely because it was filed, turn the exception into a fee waiver, or establish an actual grant or exceptional-circumstances finding. House 70015 separately adds fees for two different diversity-visa events: filing a diversity immigrant-visa application ($400 fiscal2025 minimum or higher DHS rule amount, collected at filing) and registering for that program ($250 minimum or higher rule amount, collected at registration). Both have fiscal2026-onward July-to-July CPI-U increments; ONLY the application increment expressly rounds down to$10, while the registration formula prints no rounding rule. Both applicable fees cannot be waived or reduced. Across fees received under this SECTION, 10percent is directed to detecting/preventing program fraud and offsetting program costs, and a separate10percent is credited to ICE to retain/spend without further appropriation for detention, immigration enforcement and removal operations; amounts not used or credited go to Treasury. These are not percentages of only one fee or assumed actual expenditure. Complete pre-vote1153(c) already establishes diversity visa allocation, including its five-year admission/geographic formulas, high-admission-state exclusion, regional redistribution and seven-percent state limit, and the education OR qualified-work-experience requirement. The proposal adds fees to the identified program rather than creating it, changing those allocation/eligibility rules by payment, guaranteeing selection or issuing a visa. Registration, application, selection and actual grant remain distinct; no separate component preference follows from either member's whole-package vote. House 70016 adds ten EOIR court/application/appeal/motion fee provisions. In(a)-(c), an alien's court filing OR court adjudication of the identified adjustment, inadmissibility-waiver orTPS application triggers payment at filing OR, as applicable, before court adjudication; two automatic charges for the same application are not asserted. The(d)/(e) alien appeals, (f) practitioner appeal and(g) alien motion collect at filing. The(h)-(j) provisions collect when an alien files the identified suspension, permanent-resident cancellation or nonpermanent-resident cancellation/adjustment application WITH AN IMMIGRATION COURT. House(j) identifies the application for certain nonpermanent residents without copying Senate's distinct non-LPR-payer wording. The ten listed fiscal2025 floors are separate fee events, additional to other authorized fees, with a higher AttorneyGeneral rule amount permitted: adjustment to lawful permanent residence $1,500; waiver of grounds of inadmissibility $1,050; TPS $500; appeal from an immigration-judge decision $900; appeal from a DHS-officer decision $900; practitioner disciplinary appeal $1,325; motion to reopen or reconsider an immigration-judge or Board of Immigration Appeals decision $900; suspension of deportation application $600; cancellation of removal for the specified permanent-resident category $600; and cancellation/adjustment for the specified nonpermanent-resident category $1,500. Each subsection has fiscal2026-onward July-to-July CPI-U adjustment of its own prior-year fee, with the INCREMENT rounded down to $10, not an automatically exact future price or a sum charged to every alien. The disciplinary appeal payer is a PRACTITIONER filing an appeal of an adjudicating official's decision in a practitioner disciplinary case, not every alien or every attorney. The immigration-judge appeal provision separately excludes appeals of BOND decisions. The motion-fee exception identifies only motions to REOPEN an IN-ABSENTIA removal order under240(b)(5)(C)(ii) or an in-absentia deportation order under legacy242B(c)(3)(B), with the version's own printed temporal wording retained below. Complete pre-vote1229a(b)(5)(C)(ii) allows the identified motion at any time upon demonstrating either lack of notice in accordance with1229(a)(1) OR(a)(2), OR Federal/State custody AND nonappearance through no fault of the alien. Complete historical1252b(c)(3)(B) likewise allows the identified motion at any time upon demonstrating lack of notice in accordance with its(a)(2), OR Federal/State custody AND nonappearance through no fault of the alien. The surrounding notice/address requirements remain; these are not exemptions for every missed hearing, any custody, all reopening/reconsideration motions, or the separate180-day exceptional-circumstances grounds in240(b)(5)(C)(i)/242B(c)(3)(A). A fee exception does not establish that a motion was granted or an order actually rescinded. The1995Code historical section is corroborated by the later repeal/history notice and enacted104-208: its intervening371(b)(7) changes only242B(d)(1) officer terminology, not(c)(3)(B), and its309 effective-date/transition provisions remain qualified. Current repeal metadata is not substituted for operative legacy text. House(g)(3)(B) expressly identifies242B(c)(3)(B) AS THE SECTION EXISTED prior to April1,1997; it does not impose a pre1997 motion-filing date. House(k) bars waiver or reduction of section fees, separately from the specifically printed bond/motion nonapplication exceptions. Its proceeds clauses repeatedly say fees received UNDER THIS SECTION: (a) permits not more than50percent via ExaminationsFeeAccount transfer to EOIR, while(b)-(j) each print not more than25percent on that same section-wide reference; amounts not credited goTreasury. The repeated scope/cap interaction remains an application question, not silently rewritten as independent per-fee allocations, summed shares, fixed transfers or proven spending. Complete pre-vote1356(m)-(n) establishes the existing account framework without resolving those new competing references. House(l) bars using fees received under the section to fund the Legal Orientation Program OR any successor program; it is a restriction on these receipts, not proof the program ended or all other funding was prohibited. House 10012 replaces SNAP2015(f) with its exact version of individual immigration-status conditions. The replacement is a NECESSARY individual-status condition for a member of an OTHERWISE ELIGIBLE household, not a sufficient promise of SNAP entitlement. US RESIDENCE is common to EACH of the four alternatives, AND the individual must meet at least one listed category: (A) a citizen OR NATIONAL of the UNITED STATES; (B) the defined lawful permanent-resident immigrant, retaining the express exclusion of ordinary temporary visitors/tourists/diplomats/students with no intention of abandoning foreign residence; (C) the version's own status category described below; OR (D) an individual lawfully residing in the US IN ACCORDANCE WITH a Compact of Free Association referred to in PRWORA402(b)(2)(G). Complete1101(a)(15)/(20)/(22) defines immigrant/nonimmigrant classes, unchanged lawful permanent residence and US national, without treating every lawful temporary stay or every foreign national as a listed status. Complete1612(b)(2)(G) identifies the US Compacts with the Federated States of Micronesia, Marshall Islands and Palau; nationality alone is not substituted for the proposal's lawful-residence-under-Compact condition. The complete pre-vote2015(f) already requires residence and lists citizen/LPR, the specified1259 deemed-permanent-residence category, conditional entry under1157/1158, the described1182(d)(5) parole and withholding under1231(b)(3). The amendment replaces that subsection's list: its old conditional-entry/general-parole/withholding categories are no longer separate entries, whereas defined permanent residence remains. The new text expressly says citizen OR USnational and supplies its own(C)/(D); it is not described as the first possible benefit for USnationals or COFA residents. Complete pre-vote1611/1612/1613/1641 separately retain qualified-alien definitions, program-specific restrictions/exceptions, the qualified-status five-year framework with its exceptions, and the2024COFA provisions. Qualification alone was not a complete entitlement, nor does the selected replacement directly amend every one of those separate laws. No blanket claim that every refugee, asylee, parolee or other national loses or gains benefits is made; another independently held listed status, other applicable rules and actual eligibility determination remain distinct. The replacement RETAINS consideration of the INELIGIBLE INDIVIDUAL'S income (less a pro-rata share AT STATE OPTION) AND financial resources when determining the eligibility and allotment value of that individual's household. The State-option modifier concerns the income pro-rata subtraction, not exclusion of all financial resources or automatic termination of all household members. The prior statutory paragraph already has this calculation language; it is not a new proof of spending, a specific household's benefit amount or a benefit award. Whole-package votes do not establish component preferences. House(C) requires Cuban citizenship/nationality AND ALL four own predicates: beneficiary of an APPROVED203(a) petition; meeting ALL immigrant-visa eligibility requirements while a visa is NOT IMMEDIATELY AVAILABLE; NOT OTHERWISE INADMISSIBLE under212(a); AND PHYSICAL PRESENCE IN THE US pursuant to parole furthering the specified US commitment to annual legal Cuban migration in the1994/1995joint migration instruments. Complete pre-vote203(a) family-preference rules and the full proposal clause are bound. This is not every Cuban national, a pending petition, any parole, or an actual grant of a visa. House(C) here does NOT require living in Cuba and does not borrow the distinct House70004 parole-FEE exception's living-in-Cuba predicate. Senate's broader defined Cuban/Haitian-entrant phrase is not imported into this House list. House 44110 changes Medicaid and CHIP verification-period assistance and federal payment beginning October 1, 2026. It adds a State option under 1902(a)(46)(C) to make assistance available during the specified reasonable opportunities for citizenship/nationality or satisfactory immigration-status evidence, and during the separate Social Security inconsistency process's 90-day period. It removes the existing obligation to provide assistance during the specified documentary reasonable-opportunity periods when the State has not elected that option; the 1137(d)(4)(A)(ii)/(B)(ii) no-delay/denial/reduction/termination protection is made conditional on that election for MEDICAID, without applying that new Medicaid qualifier to every other program listed in 1137(b). The opportunity to submit evidence and the program's remaining verification processes are not themselves eliminated. New 1903(i)(22)(B) bars federal payment for amounts expended on assistance furnished under that State election during EACH specified citizenship/nationality reasonable-opportunity period, the 90-day period, or the immigration-status reasonable-opportunity period UNLESS the applicable citizenship/nationality or satisfactory immigration status is VERIFIED BY THE END OF THAT PERIOD. State election alone does not assure federal payment, and verification by the end is not described as sufficient to satisfy every other payment condition. The restriction concerns payment to the State for those expenditures, not a factual determination that missing or inconsistent proof establishes unlawful immigration status or permanent ineligibility. CHIP adds (i)(22) to its incorporated payment restrictions and applies the new State option in the same manner as Medicaid. The complete existing 1902(ee) process distinguishes the first reasonable effort to identify and address clerical/name/number/declaration inconsistencies, with assistance continued WHILE MAKING THAT EFFORT, from the subsequent unresolved-inconsistency process. House section 44110 does NOT strike that first continued-assistance clause. The subsequent 90 days run from the date the INDIVIDUAL RECEIVES the notice, not when the State sends it; that period offers documentary evidence OR resolution with Social Security, with continued assistance conditional on State election. The existing text specifies disenrollment within 30 days AFTER THE END of those 90 days using its printed no-documentary-evidence OR unresolved-inconsistency predicate; the amendment adds denial of eligibility AS APPLICABLE. Selected exact House floor State Homeland Security Grant Program and Stonegarden funding follow. House floor 60005 common appropriation: In addition to amounts otherwise available, there is appropriated to the Administrator of the Federal Emergency Management Agency, for fiscal year 2025, out of any money in the Treasury, not otherwise appropriated, to be administered under the State Homeland Security Grant Program authorized under section 2004 of the Homeland Security Act of 2002 (6 U.S.C. 605), to enhance State, local, and Tribal security through grants, contracts, cooperative agreements, and other activities, of which-- House floor 60005 purpose 1: $500,000,000, to remain available until September 30, 2029, for State and local capabilities to detect, identify, track, or monitor threats from unmanned aircraft systems (as such term is defined in section 44801 of title 49, United States Code); House floor 60005 purpose 2: $625,000,000, to remain available until September 30, 2029, for security, planning, and other costs related to the 2026 FIFA World Cup; House floor 60005 purpose 3: $1,000,000,000, to remain available until September 30, 2029, for security, planning, and other costs related to the 2028 Olympic Games and 2028 Paralympic Games; and House floor 60005 purpose 4: $450,000,000, to remain available until September 30, 2029, for the Operation Stonegarden Grant Program. The pre-vote fiscal year 2024 DHS/FEMA HSGP notice reproduced on Hawaii's official host describes Operation Stonegarden as supporting enhanced cooperation and coordination among CBP, USBP, and Federal, State, local, Tribal and territorial law enforcement agencies to improve overall border security. It funds joint border-security efforts along routes of ingress and egress to and from international borders, including travel corridors in States bordering Mexico and Canada and States and territories with international water borders. In that notice, those State, local, Tribal and territorial law enforcement agencies use their inherent law enforcement authorities and receive no additional authority from participating in Stonegarden. This is dated program-purpose context, not a new power conferred by the House appropriation or a complete 2025 eligibility rule. The floor clause appropriates to the FEMA Administrator additional fiscal year 2025 funds administered under the State Homeland Security Grant Program in 6 U.S.C. 605 for State/local/Tribal security through the printed grant, contract, cooperative-agreement and other activity paths. Each of its four purpose amounts has its own availability until September 30, 2029. The Stonegarden amount is $450,000,000. House FIFA purpose (2) expressly includes planning; House purpose (3) expressly names the 2028 Olympic Games and 2028 Paralympic Games. The Senate prints different event wording; no decision about either version's actual event-expense eligibility is inferred. The House selected text prints no Senate 90005(a)(2) FIFA/Olympics exemption or added consistent-with-titles-18-and-49 phrase. That absence is a source-version comparison, not authority to disregard otherwise applicable law. Generic drone and event funding remain adjacent context without an inferred Immigration purpose. Complete captured 603, 605 and 609 and the dated program notice are reused without changing earlier Senate meanings or declaring their every condition automatically applicable to a House-version grant. House-specific application question 53 remains separate from Senate question 52. No particular grant, entitlement, expenditure, law-enforcement power or individual status result is inferred. The floor 60005 operative body is identical to the currently governed EH 60006 body after section-title labels are removed solely for comparison. Selected exact House 110019 death/disability loan-discharge income-exclusion and SSN provisions follow. House 110019 exclusion grounds: In the case of an individual, gross income does not include any amount which (but for this subsection) would be includible in gross income for such taxable year by reason of the discharge (in whole or in part) of any loan described in subparagraph (B), if such discharge was-- (i) pursuant to subsection (a) or (d) of section 437 of the Higher Education Act of 1965 or the parallel benefit under part D of title IV of such Act (relating to the repayment of loan liability), (ii) pursuant to section 464(c)(1)(F) of such Act, or (iii) otherwise discharged on account of death or total and permanent disability of the student. House 110019 loan categories: A loan is described in this subparagraph if such loan is-- (i) a student loan (as defined in paragraph (2)), or (ii) a private education loan (as defined in section 140(a) of the Consumer Credit Protection Act (15 U.S.C. 1650(a)). House 110019 identification and own marital rules: (i) In general.--Subparagraph (A) shall not apply with respect to any discharge during any taxable year unless the taxpayer includes on the return of tax for such taxable year-- (I) the taxpayer's social security number, and (II) if the taxpayer is married, the social security number of such taxpayers's spouse. (ii) Social security number.--For purposes of this subparagraph, the term `social security number' has the meaning given such term in section 24(h)(7). (iii) Married individuals.--Rules similar to the rules of section 32(d) shall apply to this subparagraph.. House 110019 math-error amendment: Section 6213(g)(2) is amended by striking and at the end of subparagraph (U), by striking the period at the end of subparagraph (V) and inserting , and, and by inserting after subparagraph (V) the following new subparagraph: (W) an omission of a correct social security number required under section 108(f)(5)(C) (relating to discharges on account of death or disability).. House 110019 discharge-date applicability: The amendments made by this section shall apply to discharges after December 31, 2025. Each version replaces only 108(f)(5) with the printed exclusion, not all of section 108 or every student-loan tax rule. The original 2024 (5) instead covers its defined discharge categories after December 31, 2020 and before January 1, 2026; the candidate does not silently extend that entire temporary rule unchanged. The common requirement that the discharged loan meet new subparagraph (B) applies across all three ground alternatives. Interaction of that gate, complete loan definitions and the parent-borrower 437(d) reference is reserved as question 55; no blanket conclusion that every HEA discharge qualifies for tax exclusion. Original (f)(1) service-conditioned discharge and (4) named repayment-program exclusions remain separate. New loan categories retain full 108(f)(2) student-loan definition and entire 140(a) private-education definitions, including actual (a)(8) private loan, own private-lender and expense meanings and excluded credit/mortgage categories. This does not mean every education-related debt qualifies. House 110115 account establishment and instrument: The term `TRUMP account' means a trust created or organized in the United States for the exclusive benefit of an individual and which is designated (in such manner as the Secretary shall prescribe) at the time of the establishment of the trust as a TRUMP account, but only if the written governing instrument creating the trust meets the following requirements: (A) The individual establishing the account shall provide to the trustee the social security number of such individual and of the account beneficiary. (B) Except in the case of a qualified rollover contribution described in subsection (e), no contribution will be accepted-- (i) before January 1, 2026, (ii) unless it is in cash, (iii) unless the account beneficiary has not attained age 18, and (iv) if such contribution would result in aggregate contributions for the taxable year exceeding the contribution limit specified in subsection (c)(1). (C) No distribution (other than a distribution of a qualified rollover contribution) will be allowed-- (i) before the date on which the account beneficiary attains age 18, or (ii) in the case of such an account the account beneficiary of which has not attained age 25, if the aggregate distributions from such account exceeds the amount that is \1/2\ the cash equivalent value of the account on the date on which the account beneficiary attains age 18. (D) The account beneficiary has not attained age 8 on the date of the establishment of the account. (E) The trustee is a bank (as defined in section 408(n)) or another person who demonstrates to the satisfaction of the Secretary that the manner in which that person will administer the trust will be consistent with the requirements of this section or who has so demonstrated with respect to any individual retirement plan. (F) The interest of an individual in the balance of his account is nonforfeitable. (G) The assets of the trust shall not be commingled with other property except in a common trust fund or common investment fund. (H) No part of the trust funds will be invested in any asset other than eligible investments. (b) New Capital Assets .—In the fiscal year following each fiscal year for which appropriations are enacted for a new capital asset, the report submitted under subsection (a) shall include— (1) an estimated life-cycle cost estimate for the new capital asset; (2) an assessment of the impact the new capital asset will have on— (A) delivery dates for each capital asset; (B) estimated completion dates for each capital asset; (C) the total estimated cost to complete each capital asset; and (D) other planned construction or improvement projects; and (3) recommended funding levels for each capital asset necessary to meet the estimated completion dates and total estimated costs included in the such 1 asset's approved acquisition program baseline. (c) Definitions .—In this section, the term "new capital asset" means— (1) an acquisition program that does not have an approved acquisition program baseline; or (2) the acquisition of a capital asset in excess of the number included in the approved acquisition program baseline. (b) Information To Be Included .—Each report under subsection (a) shall include for each major acquisition program— (1) a statement of the Coast Guard's mission needs and performance goals relating to such program, including a justification for any change to those needs and goals subsequent to a report previously submitted under this section; (2) a justification explaining how the projected number and capabilities of assets acquired under such program meet applicable mission needs and performance goals; (3) an identification of any and all mission hour gaps, accompanied by an explanation of how and when the Coast Guard will close those gaps; (4) an identification of any changes with respect to such program, including— (A) any changes to the timeline for the acquisition of each new asset and the phaseout of legacy assets; and (B) any changes to— (i) the costs of new assets or legacy assets for that fiscal year or future fiscal years; or (ii) the total acquisition cost; (5) a justification explaining how any change to such program fulfills the mission needs and performance goals of the Coast Guard; (6) a description of how the Coast Guard is planning for the integration of each new asset acquired under such program into the Coast Guard, including needs related to shore-based infrastructure and human resources; (7) an identification of how funds in the applicable fiscal year's budget request will be allocated, including information on the purchase of specific assets; (8) a projection of the remaining operational lifespan and life-cycle cost of each legacy asset that also identifies any anticipated resource gaps; (9) a detailed explanation of how the costs of legacy assets are being accounted for within such program; and (10) an annual performance comparison of new assets to legacy assets. (c) Adequacy of Acquisition Workforce .—Each report under subsection (a) shall— (1) include information on the scope of the acquisition activities to be performed in the next fiscal year and on the adequacy of the current acquisition workforce to meet that anticipated workload; (2) specify the number of officers, members, and employees of the Coast Guard currently and planned to be assigned to each position designated under section 1102(c); 1 and (3) identify positions that are or will be understaffed and actions that will be taken to correct such understaffing. (d) Cutters Not Maintained in Class .—Each report under subsection (a) shall identify which, if any, Coast Guard cutters that have been issued a certificate of classification by the American Bureau of Shipping have not been maintained in class, with an explanation detailing the reasons why the cutters have not been maintained in class. (e) Long-term Major Acquisitions Plan .—Each report under subsection (a) shall include a plan that describes for the upcoming fiscal year, and for each of the 20 fiscal years thereafter— (1) the numbers and types of cutters and aircraft to be decommissioned; (2) the numbers and types of cutters and aircraft to be acquired to— (A) replace the cutters and aircraft identified under paragraph (1); or (B) address an identified capability gap; and (3) the estimated level of funding in each fiscal year required to— (A) acquire the cutters and aircraft identified under paragraph (2); (B) operate and sustain the cutters and aircraft described in paragraph (2); (C) acquire related command, control, communications, computer, intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance systems; and (D) acquire, construct, or renovate shoreside infrastructure. (f) Major Acquisition Program Defined .—In this section, the term "major acquisition program" means an ongoing acquisition undertaken by the Coast Guard with a life-cycle cost estimate greater than or equal to $300,000,000. House new 25F allowance: (a) Allowance of Credit.--In the case of an individual, there shall be allowed as a credit against the tax imposed by this chapter for the taxable year an amount equal to the aggregate amount of qualified contributions made by the taxpayer during the taxable year. House own contributing-taxpayer credit limits: (b) Limitations.-- (1) In general.--The credit allowed under subsection (a) to any taxpayer for any taxable year shall not exceed an amount equal to the greater of-- (A) 10 percent of the adjusted gross income of the taxpayer for the taxable year, or (B) $5,000. (2) Allocation of volume cap.--The credit allowed under subsection (a) to any taxpayer for any taxable year shall not exceed the amount of the volume cap allocated by the Secretary to such taxpayer under subsection (g) with respect to qualified contributions made by the taxpayer during the taxable year. (3) Reduction based on state credit.--The amount allowed as a credit under subsection (a) for a taxable year shall be reduced by the amount allowed as a credit on any State tax return of the taxpayer for qualified contributions made by the taxpayer during the taxable year. House own eligible-student definition: (1) Eligible student.--The term `eligible student' means an individual who-- (A) is a member of a household with an income which is not greater than 300 percent of the area median gross income (as such term is used in section 42), and (B) is eligible to enroll in a public elementary or secondary school. House own complete calendar volume-cap mechanism: (g) Volume Cap.-- (1) In general.--The volume cap applicable under this section shall be $5,000,000,000 for each of calendar years 2026 through 2029, and zero for calendar years thereafter. Such amount shall be allocated by the Secretary as provided in paragraph (2) to taxpayers with respect to qualified contributions made by such taxpayers, except that 10 percent of such amount shall be divided evenly among the States, and shall be available with respect to individuals residing in such States. (2) First-come, first-serve.--For purposes of applying the volume cap under this section, such volume cap for any calendar year shall be allocated by the Secretary on a first- come, first-serve basis, as determined based on the time (during such calendar year) at which the taxpayer made the qualified contribution with respect to which the allocation is made. The Secretary shall not make any allocation of volume cap for any calendar year after December 31 of such calendar year. (3) Real-time information.--For purposes of this section, the Secretary shall develop a system to track the amount of qualified contributions made during the calendar year for which a credit may be claimed under this section, with such information to be updated in real time. (4) Annual increases.-- (A) In general.--In the case of the calendar year after a high-use calendar year, the dollar amount otherwise in effect under paragraph (1) for such calendar year shall be equal to 105 percent of the dollar amount in effect for such high-use calendar year. (B) High-use calendar year.--For purposes of this subsection, the term `high-use calendar year' means any calendar year for which 90 percent or more of the volume cap in effect for such calendar year under paragraph (1) is allocated to taxpayers. (C) Prevention of decreases in annual volume cap.--The volume cap in effect under [[Page H2305]] paragraph (1) for any calendar year shall not be less than the volume cap in effect under such paragraph for the preceding calendar year. (D) Publication of annual volume cap.--The Secretary shall make publicly available the dollar amount of the volume cap in effect under paragraph (1) for each calendar year. (5) States.--For purposes of this subsection, the term `State' includes the District of Columbia.. House separate scholarship income exemption: (b) Exemption From Gross Income for Scholarships for Qualified Elementary or Secondary Education Expenses of Eligible Students.-- (1) In general.--Part III of subchapter B of chapter 1 is amended by inserting before section 140 the following new section: SEC. 139J. claim_source_map.passage: SEC. 60001. BORDER BARRIER SYSTEM CONSTRUCTION, INVASIVE SPECIES, AND BORDER SECURITY FACILITIES IMPROVEMENTS. In addition to amounts otherwise available, there is appropriated to the Commissioner of U.S. Customs and Border Protection for fiscal year 2025, out of any money in the Treasury not otherwise appropriated, to remain available until September 30, 2029, the following: (1) $46,500,000,000 for necessary expenses relating to the following: (A) Construction, installation, or improvement of primary, waterborne, and secondary barriers. (B) Access roads. (C) Barrier system attributes, including cameras, lights, sensors, roads, and other detection technology. claim_source_map.locator: 60004: exact manager-added State reimbursement conditions
claim_source_map.passage: SEC. 60004. STATE BORDER SECURITY REIMBURSEMENT. (a) In General.--In addition to amounts otherwise available, there is appropriated to the Secretary of Homeland Security, for fiscal year 2025, out of any money in the Treasury not otherwise appropriated, $12,000,000,000, to remain available until September 30, 2029, to carry out this section. (b) Use of Funds.--The Secretary of Homeland Security shall use amounts made available under subsection (a) to make grants to States for costs associated with actions taken on or after January 21, 2021, to assist the Federal border security missions to enforce the immigration laws, including through detention and removal, and to combat the unlawful entry of persons and contraband. (c) Application.--The Secretary of Homeland Security shall develop a process for States to submit a grant application, together with satisfactory evidence of costs incurred, to seek reimbursement for any expenses described in subsection (b). (d) Prohibition.--The Secretary of Homeland Security may not make a grant for reimbursement under this section to a State if such State has received such reimbursement under any other grant program of the Department of Homeland Security.

claim_source_map.locator: 70101: complete detention amount, permission, definitions and standards
claim_source_map.passage: SEC. 70101. ADULT ALIEN DETENTION CAPACITY AND FAMILY RESIDENTIAL CENTERS. (a) Appropriation.--In addition to amounts otherwise available, there is appropriated to U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement for fiscal year 2025, out of any money in the Treasury not otherwise appropriated, $45,000,000,000 to remain available until September 30, 2029, for the purposes described in subsection (b). (b) Use of Funds.--Amounts made available under subsection (a) shall only be used for family residential center capacity and single adult alien detention capacity. (c) Duration.--The Department of Homeland Security may detain family units of aliens at family residential centers, as described in subsections (b) and (d), pending a decision on whether the aliens are to be removed from the United States and, if such aliens are ordered removed from the United States, until such aliens are removed. (d) Family Residential Center Defined.--In this section, the term ``family residential center'' means a facility used by the Department of Homeland Security to detain family units of aliens (including alien children who are not unaccompanied alien children) who are encountered or apprehended by the Department of Homeland Security, regardless of whether the facility is licensed by the State or a political subdivision of the State in which the facility is located. (e) Detention Standards.--To efficiently utilize the funding appropriated by this section, the detention standards for the single adult detention capacity described in subsection (b) shall be set in the sole discretion of the Secretary of Homeland Security.

claim_source_map.locator: 70001-70002: exact fee applicability, floor, inflation, proceeds and waiver
claim_source_map.passage: SEC. 70001. APPLICABILITY OF THE IMMIGRATION LAWS. (a) Applicability.--Notwithstanding any provision of the immigration laws (as defined under section 101 of the Immigration and Nationality Act), the fees under this subtitle shall apply. (b) Terms.--The terms used under this subtitle shall have the meanings given such terms in section 101 of the Immigration and Nationality Act. (c) References to Immigration and Nationality Act.--Except as otherwise expressly provided, whenever this subtitle references a section or other provision, the reference shall be considered to be to a section or other provision of the Immigration and Nationality Act. SEC. 70002. ASYLUM FEE. (a) In General.--In addition to any other fee authorized by law, the Secretary of Homeland Security or the Attorney General, as applicable, shall impose a fee in the amount specified in this section for a fiscal year on each alien who files an application for asylum under section 208 of the Immigration and Nationality Act at the time such application is filed. (b) Initial Amount.--The amount specified in this section for fiscal year 2025 shall be such amount as the Secretary or Attorney General, as applicable, may by rule provide, but in any event not less than $1,000. (c) Subsequent Adjustment.--Beginning in fiscal year 2026 and each fiscal year thereafter, the amount specified in this section for a fiscal year shall be equal to the sum of-- (1) the amount imposed under this section for the prior fiscal year; and (2) rounded to the next lowest multiple of $10, the amount referred to in paragraph (1), multiplied by the percentage (if any) by which the Consumer Price Index for All Urban Consumers for the month of July preceding the date on which such adjustment takes effect exceeds the Consumer Price Index for All Urban Consumers for the same month of the preceding calendar year. (d) Crediting Certain Funds.--During any fiscal year, the total amount of fees received under this section shall be subject to the following: (1) 50 percent of fees received from applications filed with the Attorney General shall be credited to the Executive Office for Immigration Review to retain and spend without further appropriation. (2) 50 percent of fees received from applications filed with the Secretary of Homeland Security shall be credited to U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services and deposited into the Immigration Examinations Fee Account established under section 286(m) of the Immigration and Nationality Act (8 U.S.C. 1356(m)) to retain and spend without further appropriation. (3) Any amounts not credited to the Executive Office for Immigration Review or U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services shall be deposited into the general fund of the Treasury. (e) No Waiver.--A fee imposed under this section shall not be waived or reduced.

(b) Use of Funds.--The Secretary of Homeland Security shall use amounts made available under subsection (a) to make grants to States for costs associated with actions taken on or after January 21, 2021, to assist the Federal border security missions to enforce the immigration laws, including through detention and removal, and to combat the unlawful entry of persons and contraband. (c) Application.--The Secretary of Homeland Security shall develop a process for States to submit a grant application, together with satisfactory evidence of costs incurred, to seek reimbursement for any expenses described in subsection (b). (d) Prohibition.--The Secretary of Homeland Security may not make a grant for reimbursement under this section to a State if such State has received such reimbursement under any other grant program of the Department of Homeland Security.

claim_source_map.passage: §279. Children's affairs (a) Transfer of functions There are transferred to the Director of the Office of Refugee Resettlement of the Department of Health and Human Services functions under the immigration laws of the United States with respect to the care of unaccompanied alien children that were vested by statute in, or performed by, the Commissioner of Immigration and Naturalization (or any officer, employee, or component of the Immigration and Naturalization Service) immediately before the effective date specified in subsection (d). (b) Functions (1) In general Pursuant to the transfer made by subsection (a), the Director of the Office of Refugee Resettlement shall be responsible for— (A) coordinating and implementing the care and placement of unaccompanied alien children who are in Federal custody by reason of their immigration status, including developing a plan to be submitted to Congress on how to ensure that qualified and independent legal counsel is timely appointed to represent the interests of each such child, consistent with the law regarding appointment of counsel that is in effect on November 25, 2002; (B) ensuring that the interests of the child are considered in decisions and actions relating to the care and custody of an unaccompanied alien child; (C) making placement determinations for all unaccompanied alien children who are in Federal custody by reason of their immigration status; (D) implementing the placement determinations; (E) implementing policies with respect to the care and placement of unaccompanied alien children; (F) identifying a sufficient number of qualified individuals, entities, and facilities to house unaccompanied alien children; (G) overseeing the infrastructure and personnel of facilities in which unaccompanied alien children reside; (H) reuniting unaccompanied alien children with a parent abroad in appropriate cases; (I) compiling, updating, and publishing at least annually a state-by-state list of professionals or other entities qualified to provide guardian and attorney representation services for unaccompanied alien children; (J) maintaining statistical information and other data on unaccompanied alien children for whose care and placement the Director is responsible, which shall include— (i) biographical information, such as a child's name, gender, date of birth, country of birth, and country of habitual residence; (ii) the date on which the child came into Federal custody by reason of his or her immigration status; (iii) information relating to the child's placement, removal, or release from each facility in which the child has resided; (iv) in any case in which the child is placed in detention or released, an explanation relating to the detention or release; and (v) the disposition of any actions in which the child is the subject; (K) collecting and compiling statistical information from the Department of Justice, the Department of Homeland Security, and the Department of State on each department's actions relating to unaccompanied alien children; and (L) conducting investigations and inspections of facilities and other entities in which unaccompanied alien children reside, including regular follow-up visits to such facilities, placements, and other entities, to assess the continued suitability of such placements. (2) Coordination with other entities; no release on own recognizance In making determinations described in paragraph (1)(C), the Director of the Office of Refugee Resettlement— (A) shall consult with appropriate juvenile justice professionals, the Director of the Bureau of Citizenship and Immigration Services, and the Assistant Secretary of the Bureau of Border Security to ensure that such determinations ensure that unaccompanied alien children described in such subparagraph— (i) are likely to appear for all hearings or proceedings in which they are involved; (ii) are protected from smugglers, traffickers, or others who might seek to victimize or otherwise engage them in criminal, harmful, or exploitive activity; and (iii) are placed in a setting in which they are not likely to pose a danger to themselves or others; and (B) shall not release such children upon their own recognizance. (3) Duties with respect to foster care In carrying out the duties described in paragraph (1), the Director of the Office of Refugee Resettlement is encouraged to use the refugee children foster care system established pursuant to section 412(d) of the Immigration and Nationality Act (8 U.S.C. 1522(d)) for the placement of unaccompanied alien children. (4) Rule of construction Nothing in paragraph (2)(B) may be construed to require that a bond be posted for an unaccompanied alien child who is released to a qualified sponsor. (c) Rule of construction Nothing in this section may be construed to transfer the responsibility for adjudicating benefit determinations under the Immigration and Nationality Act (8 U.S.C. 1101 et seq.) from the authority of any official of the Department of Justice, the Department of Homeland Security, or the Department of State. (d) Effective date Notwithstanding section 4, 1 this section shall take effect on the date on which the transfer of functions specified under section 251 of this title takes effect. (e) References With respect to any function transferred by this section, any reference in any other Federal law, Executive order, rule, regulation, or delegation of authority, or any document of or pertaining to a component of government from which such function is transferred— (1) to the head of such component is deemed to refer to the Director of the Office of Refugee Resettlement; or (2) to such component is deemed to refer to the Office of Refugee Resettlement of the Department of Health and Human Services. (f) Other transition issues (1) Exercise of authorities Except as otherwise provided by law, a Federal official to whom a function is transferred by this section may, for purposes of performing the function, exercise all authorities under any other provision of law that were available with respect to the performance of that function to the official responsible for the performance of the function immediately before the effective date specified in subsection (d). (2) Savings provisions Subsections (a), (b), and (c) of section 552 of this title shall apply to a transfer of functions under this section in the same manner as such provisions apply to a transfer of functions under this chapter to the Department of Homeland Security. (3) Transfer and allocation of appropriations and personnel The personnel of the Department of Justice employed in connection with the functions transferred by this section, and the assets, liabilities, contracts, property, records, and unexpended balance of appropriations, authorizations, allocations, and other funds employed, held, used, arising from, available to, or to be made available to, the Immigration and Naturalization Service in connection with the functions transferred by this section, subject to section 1531 of title 31, shall be transferred to the Director of the Office of Refugee Resettlement for allocation to the appropriate component of the Department of Health and Human Services. Unexpended funds transferred pursuant to this paragraph shall be used only for the purposes for which the funds were originally authorized and appropriated. (g) Definitions As used in this section— (1) the term "placement" means the placement of an unaccompanied alien child in either a detention facility or an alternative to such a facility; and (2) the term "unaccompanied alien child" means a child who— (A) has no lawful immigration status in the United States; (B) has not attained 18 years of age; and (C) with respect to whom— (i) there is no parent or legal guardian in the United States; or (ii) no parent or legal guardian in the United States is available to provide care and physical custody. (Pub. L. 107–296, title IV, §462, Nov. 25, 2002, 116 Stat. 2202; Pub. L. 110–457, title II, §235(f), Dec. 23, 2008, 122 Stat. 5081.)

Such fees shall not exceed the Attorney General's costs in adjudicating the applications. The Attorney General may provide for the assessment and payment of such fees over a period of time or by installments.
