claim_source_map.passage: §6418. Transfer of certain credits (a) In general In the case of an eligible taxpayer which elects to transfer all (or any portion specified in the election) of an eligible credit determined with respect to such taxpayer for any taxable year to a taxpayer (referred to in this section as the "transferee taxpayer") which is not related (within the meaning of section 267(b) or 707(b)(1)) to the eligible taxpayer, the transferee taxpayer specified in such election (and not the eligible taxpayer) shall be treated as the taxpayer for purposes of this title with respect to such credit (or such portion thereof). (b) Treatment of payments made in connection with transfer With respect to any amount paid by a transferee taxpayer to an eligible taxpayer as consideration for a transfer described in subsection (a), such consideration— (1) shall be required to be paid in cash, (2) shall not be includible in gross income of the eligible taxpayer, and (3) with respect to the transferee taxpayer, shall not be deductible under this title. (c) Application to partnerships and S corporations (1) In general In the case of any eligible credit determined with respect to any facility or property held directly by a partnership or S corporation, if such partnership or S corporation makes an election under subsection (a) (in such manner as the Secretary may provide) with respect to such credit— (A) any amount received as consideration for a transfer described in such subsection shall be treated as tax exempt income for purposes of sections 705 and 1366, and (B) a partner's distributive share of such tax exempt income shall be based on such partner's distributive share of the otherwise eligible credit for each taxable year. (2) Coordination with application at partner or shareholder level In the case of any facility or property held directly by a partnership or S corporation, no election by any partner or shareholder shall be allowed under subsection (a) with respect to any eligible credit determined with respect to such facility or property. (d) Taxable year in which credit taken into account In the case of any credit (or portion thereof) with respect to which an election is made under subsection (a), such credit shall be taken into account in the first taxable year of the transferee taxpayer ending with, or after, the taxable year of the eligible taxpayer with respect to which the credit was determined. (e) Limitations on election (1) Time for election An election under subsection (a) to transfer any portion of an eligible credit shall be made not later than the due date (including extensions of time) for the return of tax for the taxable year for which the credit is determined, but in no event earlier than 180 days after the date of the enactment of this section. Any such election, once made, shall be irrevocable. (2) No additional transfers No election may be made under subsection (a) by a transferee taxpayer with respect to any portion of an eligible credit which has been previously transferred to such taxpayer pursuant to this section. (f) Definitions For purposes of this section— (1) Eligible credit (A) In general The term "eligible credit" means each of the following: (i) So much of the credit for alternative fuel vehicle refueling property allowed under section 30C which, pursuant to subsection (d)(1) of such section, is treated as a credit listed in section 38(b). (ii) The renewable electricity production credit determined under section 45(a). (iii) The credit for carbon oxide sequestration determined under section 45Q(a). (iv) The zero-emission nuclear power production credit determined under section 45U(a). (v) The clean hydrogen production credit determined under section 45V(a). (vi) The advanced manufacturing production credit determined under section 45X(a). (vii) The clean electricity production credit determined under section 45Y(a). (viii) The clean fuel production credit determined under section 45Z(a). (ix) The energy credit determined under section 48. (x) The qualifying advanced energy project credit determined under section 48C. (xi) The clean electricity investment credit determined under section 48E. (B) Election for certain credits In the case of any eligible credit described in clause (ii), (iii), (v), or (vii) of subpara graph (A), an election under subsection (a) shall be made— (i) separately with respect to each facility for which such credit is determined, and (ii) for each taxable year during the 10-year period beginning on the date such facility was originally placed in service (or, in the case of the credit described in clause (iii), for each year during the 12-year period beginning on the date the carbon capture equipment was originally placed in service at such facility). (C) Exception for business credit carryforwards or carrybacks The term "eligible credit" shall not include any business credit carryforward or business credit carryback determined under section 39. (2) Eligible taxpayer The term "eligible taxpayer" means any taxpayer which is not described in section 6417(d)(1)(A). (g) Special rules For purposes of this section— (1) Additional information As a condition of, and prior to, any transfer of any portion of an eligible credit pursuant to subsection (a), the Secretary may require such information (including, in such form or manner as is determined appropriate by the Secretary, such information returns) or registration as the Secretary deems necessary for purposes of preventing duplication, fraud, improper payments, or excessive payments under this section. (2) Excessive credit transfer (A) In general In the case of any portion of an eligible credit which is transferred to a transferee taxpayer pursuant to subsection (a) which the Secretary determines constitutes an excessive credit transfer, the tax imposed on the transferee taxpayer by chapter 1 (regardless of whether such entity would otherwise be subject to tax under such chapter) for the taxable year in which such determination is made shall be increased by an amount equal to the sum of— (i) the amount of such excessive credit transfer, plus (ii) an amount equal to 20 percent of such excessive credit transfer. (B) Reasonable cause Subparagraph (A)(ii) shall not apply if the transferee taxpayer demonstrates to the satisfaction of the Secretary that the excessive credit transfer resulted from reasonable cause. (C) Excessive credit transfer defined For purposes of this paragraph, the term "excessive credit transfer" means, with respect to a facility or property for which an election is made under subsection (a) for any taxable year, an amount equal to the excess of— (i) the amount of the eligible credit claimed by the transferee taxpayer with respect to such facility or property for such taxable year, over (ii) the amount of such credit which, without application of this section, would be otherwise allowable under this title with respect to such facility or property for such taxable year. (3) Basis reduction; notification of recapture In the case of any election under subsection (a) with respect to any portion of an eligible credit described in clauses (ix) through (xi) of subsection (f)(1)(A)— (A) subsection (c) of section 50 shall apply to the applicable investment credit property (as defined in subsection (a)(5) of such section) as if such eligible credit was allowed to the eligible taxpayer, and (B) if, during any taxable year, the applicable investment credit property (as defined in subsection (a)(5) of section 50) is disposed of, or otherwise ceases to be investment credit property with respect to the eligible taxpayer, before the close of the recapture period (as described in subsection (a)(1) of such section)— (i) such eligible taxpayer shall provide notice of such occurrence to the transferee taxpayer (in such form and manner as the Secretary shall prescribe), and (ii) the transferee taxpayer shall provide notice of the recapture amount (as defined in subsection (c)(2) of such section), if any, to the eligible taxpayer (in such form and manner as the Secretary shall prescribe). (4) Prohibition on election or transfer with respect to progress expenditures This section shall not apply with respect to any amount of an eligible credit which is allowed pursuant to rules similar to the rules of subsections (c)(4) and (d) of section 46 (as in effect on the day before the date of the enactment of the Revenue Reconciliation Act of 1990). (h) Regulations The Secretary shall issue such regulations or other guidance as may be necessary to carry out the purposes of this section, including regulations or other guidance providing rules for determining a partner's distributive share of the tax exempt income described in subsection (c)(1).

Visa-integrity reimbursement is discretionary and available only after the visa period of validity expires. House requires demonstration of one of three alternatives: no admission sought during that validity period; or compliance with all visa conditions after admission, including no unauthorized employment, together with departure no later than five days after the date authorized to remain; or filing to extend, change or adjust status within visa validity. Senate requires post-admission compliance with all visa conditions in BOTH alternatives, including no unauthorized employment, together with either (A) no request to extend the period of admission during the visa validity period AND departure no later than five days after the last day of "such period", or (B) a GRANTED nonimmigrant extension or adjustment to lawful permanent resident status during the visa validity period. The printed Senate "such period" referent remains a separate application question. Filing is not a grant; visa validity is not admission duration; the five-day reimbursement conditions do not establish general stay/work permission.

House 110115 account establishment and instrument: The term `TRUMP account' means a trust created or organized in the United States for the exclusive benefit of an individual and which is designated (in such manner as the Secretary shall prescribe) at the time of the establishment of the trust as a TRUMP account, but only if the written governing instrument creating the trust meets the following requirements: (A) The individual establishing the account shall provide to the trustee the social security number of such individual and of the account beneficiary. (B) Except in the case of a qualified rollover contribution described in subsection (e), no contribution will be accepted-- (i) before January 1, 2026, (ii) unless it is in cash, (iii) unless the account beneficiary has not attained age 18, and (iv) if such contribution would result in aggregate contributions for the taxable year exceeding the contribution limit specified in subsection (c)(1). (C) No distribution (other than a distribution of a qualified rollover contribution) will be allowed-- (i) before the date on which the account beneficiary attains age 18, or (ii) in the case of such an account the account beneficiary of which has not attained age 25, if the aggregate distributions from such account exceeds the amount that is \1/2\ the cash equivalent value of the account on the date on which the account beneficiary attains age 18. (D) The account beneficiary has not attained age 8 on the date of the establishment of the account. (E) The trustee is a bank (as defined in section 408(n)) or another person who demonstrates to the satisfaction of the Secretary that the manner in which that person will administer the trust will be consistent with the requirements of this section or who has so demonstrated with respect to any individual retirement plan. (F) The interest of an individual in the balance of his account is nonforfeitable. (G) The assets of the trust shall not be commingled with other property except in a common trust fund or common investment fund. (H) No part of the trust funds will be invested in any asset other than eligible investments. Senate own new 25F clause a: (a) Allowance of Credit.--In the case of an individual who is a citizen or resident of the United States (within the meaning of section 7701(a)(9)), there shall be allowed as a credit against the tax imposed by this chapter for the taxable year an amount equal to the aggregate amount of qualified contributions made by the taxpayer during the taxable year. Senate own new 25F clause b: (b) Limitations.-- (1) In general.--The credit allowed under subsection (a) to any taxpayer for any taxable year shall not exceed $1,700. (2) Reduction based on state credit.--The amount allowed as a credit under subsection (a) for a taxable year shall be reduced by the amount allowed as a credit on any State tax return of the taxpayer for qualified contributions made by the taxpayer during the taxable year. Senate own new 25F clause c: (c) Definitions.--For purposes of this section-- (1) Covered state.--The term `covered State' means one of the States, or the District of Columbia, that, for a calendar year, voluntarily elects to participate under this section and to identify scholarship granting organizations in the State, in accordance with subsection (g). (2) Eligible student.--The term `eligible student' means an individual who-- (A) is a member of a household with an income which, for the calendar year prior to the date of the application for a scholarship, is not greater than 300 percent of the area median gross income (as such term is used in section 42), and (B) is eligible to enroll in a public elementary or secondary school. (3) Qualified contribution.--The term `qualified contribution' means a charitable contribution of cash to a scholarship granting organization that uses the contribution to fund scholarships for eligible students solely within the State in which the organization is listed pursuant to subsection (g). (4) Qualified elementary or secondary education expense.--The term `qualified elementary or secondary education expense' means any expense of an eligible student which is described in section 530(b)(3)(A). (5) Scholarship granting organization.--The term `scholarship granting organization' means any organization-- (A) which-- (i) is described in section 501(c)(3) and exempt from tax under section 501(a), and (ii) is not a private foundation, (B) which prevents the co-mingling of qualified contributions with other amounts by maintaining one or more separate accounts exclusively for qualified contributions, (C) which satisfies the requirements of subsection (d), and (D) which is included on the list submitted for the applicable covered State under subsection (g) for the applicable year. Senate own new 25F clause d: (d) Requirements for Scholarship Granting Organizations.-- (1) In general.--An organization meets the requirements of this subsection if-- (A) such organization provides scholarships to 10 or more students who do not all attend the same school, (B) such organization spends not less than 90 percent of the income of the organization on scholarships for eligible students, (C) such organization does not provide scholarships for any expenses other than qualified elementary or secondary education expenses, (D) such organization provides a scholarship to eligible students with a priority for-- (i) students awarded a scholarship the previous school year, and (ii) after application of clause (i), any eligible students who have a sibling who was awarded a scholarship from such organization, (E) such organization does not earmark or set aside contributions for scholarships on behalf of any particular student, and (F) such organization-- (i) verifies the annual household income and family size of eligible students who apply for scholarships to ensure such students meet the requirement of subsection (c)(2)(A), and (ii) limits the awarding of scholarships to eligible students who are a member of a household for which the income does not exceed the amount established under subsection (c)(2)(A). (2) Prohibition on self-dealing.-- (A) In general.--A scholarship granting organization may not award a scholarship to any disqualified person. (B) Disqualified person.--For purposes of this paragraph, a disqualified person shall be determined pursuant to rules similar to the rules of section 4946. Senate own new 25F clause e: (e) Denial of Double Benefit.--Any qualified contribution for which a credit is allowed under this section shall not be taken into account as a charitable contribution for purposes of section 170. Senate own new 25F clause f: (f) Carryforward of Unused Credit.-- (1) In general.--If the credit allowable under subsection (a) for any taxable year exceeds the limitation imposed by section 26(a) for such taxable year reduced by the sum of the credits allowable under this subpart (other than this section, section 23, and section 25D), such excess shall be carried to the succeeding taxable year and added to the credit allowable under subsection (a) for such taxable year. (2) Limitation.--No credit may be carried forward under this subsection to any taxable year following the fifth taxable year after the taxable year in which the credit arose. For purposes of the preceding sentence, credits shall be treated as used on a first-in first-out basis. Senate own new 25F clause g: (g) State List of Scholarship Granting Organizations.-- (1) List.-- (A) In general.--Not later than January 1 of each calendar year (or, with respect to the first calendar year for which this section applies, as early as practicable), a State that voluntarily elects to participate under this section shall provide to the Secretary a list of the scholarship granting organizations that meet the requirements described in subsection (c)(5) and are located in the State. house:119:1:190.candidate_short_description: H.R.1 Senate replacement: selected border, detention and asylum, employment-authorization and selected sponsor/enforcement fees
house:119:1:190.candidate_compact_description: Selected Senate H.R. 1 provisions would fund border infrastructure and detention, set fiscal 2025 asylum filing/pending fee floors of $100 each and specified asylum/parole/TPS employment-authorization initial/renewal fee floors of $550/$275, with distinct duration and termination rules. This is a whole-replacement concurrence choice, with qualifications.
candidate_shared_limitations: Selected Immigration highlights do not inventory every immigration-related benefit, tax, fee, child-sponsor or enforcement provision. This is a whole multi-domain replacement choice; no separate component preference or preferred alternative is established.

EAS90003 explicitly qualifies single-adult detention standards by applicable law and lacks the House's express State-licensing-independent language. It cannot inherit House70101's exact wording. Permission and funding do not prove universal detention, removal or legal enforceability.

Listed border and detention appropriations are additional fiscal2025 amounts available until September30,2029. The $46.55billion border account has its own scope; it is not described as every package dollar or an actual expenditure.

Initial filing and annual pending-application fees are separate charges, each with a fiscal2025 $100 floor, possible higher rule amount and no waiver/reduction. Pending fees trigger for each calendar year pending; their CPI increment rounds down to the nearest dollar, while filing-fee increments round down to $10.

The existing pre-vote fee paragraph already permits charges; MAY-to-SHALL and replacement of later sentences are the proposed changes. This explanation does not treat the subsequently enacted PublicLaw119-21 or later implementation as the July3baseline.

Exact Senate EAS controls concurrence, rather than introduced/reported/EH or later ENR/PL versions. Earlier House passage and later Senate-replacement concurrence remain one episode with distinct meanings and ordered observations, without an inferred trajectory.

Employment-authorization fees/durations concern specified initial or renewed/extended documents; they do not themselves confer work permission, end TPS or grant parole. Pre-vote1158(d)(2) no-entitlement/regulation/180day condition and1254a(a) continuingTPS work authority are retained. Whole-package observations do not establish support/opposition to any fee or duration component.

House initial and renewal/extension document limits are at most six months; Senate parole/TPS initial limits are one year or status duration, whichever shorter. Asylum-initial/renewal Senate sections do not print the House six-month sentence. Asylum-renewal House550/Senate275floors have no printed annual CPI rule; other listed EAD fees preserve their separate annual10dollar-rounded increments. Termination exceptions remain; only House prints the extra post-termination remand prohibition.

Printed EAD allocation/antecedent issues remain application questions: House70003(a)(4) uses UNDER THIS SECTION while parole/TPS fee clauses say Treasury; Senate100010 says renewal/extension OF SUCH PAROLE in its duration sentence. Preserve the source words, not a silently resolved interpretation.

Selected enforcement fees distinguish a prior in-absentia removal order PLUS later ICE arrest from an inadmissible person apprehended BETWEEN ports. Fiscal2025floors5000 may be higher by rule with separately printed CPI increments. Rescinded-order exception and notice/address/exceptional-circumstances/reopening-stay baseline remain. No new removal ground or actual order/arrest/collection follows from a package vote.

Senate100017 printedc/d proceeds clauses conflict (50percentICE/restTreasury versusALLTreasury) in both exactHTML/PDF; candidate states both without resolving application. That section prints no express waiver bar; no waiver availability is inferred. House CBP actor/waiver language is not copied to Senate. Selected sponsor/fee highlights do not establish exhaustive component coverage.

Parole-entry fees preserve all printed medical/family/transplant/adoption/temporary-return/hearing/law-enforcement predicates, not generic humanitarian labels. House Cuba-residence/family-visa/program conjunction differs from Senate granted-Cuban/Haitianentrant condition with its full definition. Exceptions and waiver bars are distinct; neither fee payment nor an exception creates parole/admission/status or an actual exemption.

HouseSIJ500minimum is conditional on its one-viable-parent/other-nonviable predicate; SenateSIJ250minimum namesalien/parent/legalguardian and lacks that House condition/expresswaiverbar. Existing complete1101(a)(27)(J), not(a)(15)(J), supplies court/best-interest/consent/parentage qualifications; no UACage rule, duplicate-payer charges or waiver availability inferred.

HouseTPS500additionalminimum has the exact non-admission/lapsed-nonimmigrant predicate. Senate raises existing50registrationMAXIMUMto500 and retainsreasonableMAY authority; do not substitute a universal500charge or copy the House floor/status scope. Its addedTreasury sentence coexists with an unstruck appropriation-credit baseline sentence, preserved as an application question. EADfees/status grant/duration and registration fee authority remain distinct.

Visa-integrity reimbursement is discretionary and available only after the visa period of validity expires. House requires demonstration of one of three alternatives: no admission sought during that validity period; or compliance with all visa conditions after admission, including no unauthorized employment, together with departure no later than five days after the date authorized to remain; or filing to extend, change or adjust status within visa validity. Senate requires post-admission compliance with all visa conditions in BOTH alternatives, including no unauthorized employment, together with either (A) no request to extend the period of admission during the visa validity period AND departure no later than five days after the last day of "such period", or (B) a GRANTED nonimmigrant extension or adjustment to lawful permanent resident status during the visa validity period. The printed Senate "such period" referent remains a separate application question. Filing is not a grant; visa validity is not admission duration; the five-day reimbursement conditions do not establish general stay/work permission.

I-94 fees attach to any-alien form application, not necessarily every entry or only land ports. The existing account deposit and appropriations refund do not create applicant refund rights. Preserve House lack of express CPI rounding versus Senate nearest-dollar increment rounding, 20-percent CBP account share and Treasury remainder separately from the visa fee.

ESTA has separate existing $17, full-cost-recovery-with-new-$10-minimum and new-at-least-$13 components. The extended sunset concerns only clause(i)(I). Both CPI amendments name clause(i)(II) but retain broader literal prior-base references; application is reserved, with no guessed fee total or increment-rounding rule. Selected House70017 edits dispositions; selected Senate100014 does not assign new(i)(III) by name. Do not transfer House account terms or EVUS waiver language into that Senate section; other package funding coverage remains partial.

House70018 retains commercial-aircraft/vessel passenger inspection or preinspection events. One exception requires BOTH transit to an outside-US destination and no immigration inspection. A separate exception covers immigration inspection AT DESIGNATED PORTS OF ENTRY for BOTH following arrival types: (a) a ferry meeting the retained non-ocean/non-coastwise, only-deck-passenger-and/or-vehicle, short frequent direct-route and public bridge/tunnel-service definition; or (b) Great Lakes vessels on the Great Lakes and connecting waterways WHEN OPERATING ON A REGULAR SCHEDULE. The designated-port condition applies in either arrival branch; each branch keeps its own definition/location/schedule conditions. Removing the geographical-origin exemption and replacing the separate $3 vessel charge are distinct edits. The new $1 Treasury sentence and unstruck all-(d)-receipts account baseline remain an application question, not a resolved distribution or applicant refund.

EVUS fees apply at enrollment only to aliens subject to EVUS; neither a fee nor payment expands System eligibility or grants admission/status. House deducts $5 per enrollment, while Senate deducts $5 times payments collected; do not equate those units silently. $30 is a fiscal2025 minimum/higher-rule boundary, CPI increments round down to$0.25, waiver bars apply to EVUS and account spending permission does not prove actual expenditure.

EOIR100013 has TEN distinct fee events and fiscal2025 minimum/higher-rule amounts, each own annual CPI increment rounded DOWN to$10. Court application filing OR applicable prior adjudication is distinct from appeal/motion filing; no automatic double charge. Practitioner disciplinary appeals charge the filing PRACTITIONER. The bond-appeal exception and the narrow IN-ABSENTIA REOPENING motions remain separate: upon DEMONSTRATION of (lack of the specifically required notice) OR (Federal/State custody AND nonappearance through no fault), not any custody/missed hearing or all motions/reconsideration/180-day exceptional-circumstances claims. No fee or exception grants relief or rescinds an order. Senate(j) keeps a NON-LPR payer at court filing of a cancellation/adjustment application FOR ANY ALIEN. Its shortened legacy PRIOR TO APRIL1,1997 date wording remains unresolved; do not assert a filing cutoff or delete the date. All(a)-(j) account-transfer caps are not-more-than25percent of the OWN SUBSECTION fees, not House50percent/SECTION shares or proven transfers. No express section-wide waiver bar is printed here; neither Housebar nor waiver availability is inferred. The Legal Orientation Program OR successor restriction concerns the identified section fees expended BY EOIR, not a demonstrated termination or every funding source.

SNAP10108 requires BOTH US RESIDENCE (common to EACH alternative) AND at least ONE own listed status: UScitizen OR USnational; definedLPR; version-specific(C); OR lawful USresidence INACCORDANCEWITH a referencedCOFA. An OTHERWISE ELIGIBLE household remains required; listed status alone does not grant benefits. Senate(C) retains HASBEENGRANTED definedCuban/Haitian-entrant status. Definitioncategory(1) specialparole/subsequent specialstatus retains regardless-of-status-at-assistance wording. Category(2) OTHER Cuban/Haitian nationals require (parole with NO otheracquiredINAstatus OR removalproceedings OR pendingasylum) AND NO final/nonappealable/legally-enforceable removalorder; each modifier stays in its own category/alternative. Nationality alone, Housepetition/program conditions or service-time wording do not prove this granted-status predicate. The rewritten(f) replaces its old list, not every separate public-benefit law or every person's full eligibility. Existing qualified-status/program restrictions/exceptions and2024COFA framework remain source-bound; no firstCOFA eligibility or blanket refugee/parolee outcome is claimed. The INELIGIBLE INDIVIDUAL'S income (less pro-rata share AT STATE OPTION) AND resources remain counted for that household's eligibility/allotment; the option concerns income subtraction, not automatic whole-household disqualification or all-resource exclusion.

Senate section 71109 begins October 1, 2026. Except for existing (v)(2)/(v)(4), State payment requires residence in a State, DC or a US territory for every listed status alternative. The individual must also satisfy at least one listed category: US citizen or US national; defined LPR; an alien who has been granted defined Cuban/Haitian entrant status; or lawful US residence under a referenced COFA. The residence requirement applies in each case. It is necessary for State payment, not sufficient individual eligibility. Emergency care requires necessity AND otherwise eligible AND no transplant; the lawfully residing child UNDER 21/pregnancy-category exception requires State election and otherwise eligibility, with its own sponsor/redetermination rules. Printed pregnancy timing is not a universal postpartum cutoff. Entrant definition modifiers remain in their own branches, not nationality-only eligibility. CHIP's own exception concerns payments for children's health-services initiatives under 2105(a)(1)(D)(ii), not a general pregnancy or all-CHIP exception; incorporated section 71103(b) amendment order is bound. CMS receives a fiscal year 2026 $15 million appropriation available until expended, not proven expenditure. Neither clause supplies the other version's assistance/rate rule, resolves every individual benefit determination or closes the whole package; FMAP clauses are separate from this verification/status description.

Senate section 71110 begins October 1, 2026. NOTWITHSTANDING (y)/(z), matching for 1903(v)(2) care furnished to an alien described in (v)(1) SHALL NOT EXCEED that State's 1905(b) percentage. Emergency necessity AND otherwise eligibility AND no transplant remain; the emergency exception is not terminated. It is not a universal 50-percent rate, every service, an automatic rate equal to the cap, or the House's 80-percent specified-State rule. The CMS fiscal year 2026 $1 million appropriation remains available until expended, without proving expenditure or savings. This remains a qualified whole-package candidate component, without a component preference, individual award or full-package closure.

Medicare section 1899C requires ONE own listed category: US citizen OR US national; lawful permanent residence; version-specific category(3); OR lawful US residence under a referenced COFA. The new list has NO NEW COMMON RESIDENCE modifier across all alternatives. Separate existing entitlement/enrollment predicates remain; the existing five-year LPR residence rule retains its own enrollment path, not every citizen or insured-benefit path. Listed status alone is not sufficient. Senate category(3) retains HAS BEEN GRANTED defined Cuban/Haitian entrant status, with each definition modifier in its own category/alternative; no House petition/program substitution or nationality-only grant. For those entitled/enrolled AS OF ENACTMENT, the restriction begins EIGHTEEN MONTHS AFTER ENACTMENT, with review completed within ONE YEAR of enactment. EACH person identified as outside ALL four categories receives notice as soon as practicable AFTER IDENTIFICATION, designed for comprehension and naming the enactment-relative termination date. Review, notice and termination are distinct; the grace is not from notice, a guaranteed minimum notice period, every later applicant or perpetual grandfathering. No vote-date/later-law calendar substitution, actual review/termination, individual award or whole-package closure follows.

ACA status treatment concerns a LAWFULLY PRESENT ALIEN who IS AND IS REASONABLY EXPECTED FOR THE ENTIRE CREDIT-ENROLLMENT PERIOD to hold an own listed LPR, version-specific Cuban-related or COFA status; these conditions are common to each alternative. Citizens/US nationals retain the separate existing condition. Status alone does not satisfy all credit/program requirements. Senate prints IF and requires HAS BEEN GRANTED defined entrant status, with own definition branches and the whole-period expectation; no House conjunction or IF AND ONLY IF repair. Its selected attestation/payment extension concerns credits; it has no direct House counterpart for 1402(e)/1331 status amendments. No continuing award or resolved residual program effect is inferred. Both credit restrictions retain the named section 151 tax-family condition (including taxpayer/spouse), INDIVIDUAL premium attribution and family-size/household-income calculations, not automatic whole-household loss or an insurance-enrollment ban. Both delete the special rule requiring ALL income NOT GREATER THAN 100 percent, lawful presence and Medicaid ineligibility BY REASON OF ALIEN STATUS. This does not alone prove credit loss at EXACTLY 100 percent, where the ordinary floor begins. The repeal starts taxable years after December 31, 2025; the status changes use taxable years after December 31, 2026 versus conforming PLAN YEARS on/after January 1, 2027. Senate lacks those direct conforming deletions/renumbering; application of the retained reference to deleted 36B(c)(1)(B) remains RESERVED. The 5000A(d)(3) reference change does not amend the existing zero monetary penalty components. No actual award, revived penalty, whole-package closure or component preference follows.

Exchange verification concerns INDIVIDUAL CREDIT COVERAGE MONTHS, not an enrollment ban: failure of this paragraph ALONE does NOT make an individual ineligible to enroll. Applicant PROVIDED OR VERIFIED information applies TO THE EXTENT RELEVANT. Senate requires enrollment AND advance-credit verification, with NO House cost-sharing third prong, HOUSEHOLD INCOME AND FAMILY SIZE and WHETHER AN ELIGIBLE ALIEN. Past-month verification prints IF. Secretary MAY waive ONLY (A) for one or more tax-year months enrolled during an SEP BASED ON CHANGE IN OWN FAMILY SIZE. ANY available data AND RELIABLE third-party sources remain FOR VERIFICATION BY THE APPLICANT. Exact June 25, 2025 final-rule(iii), printed 2026 ONLY, is expressly applied as though to ALL PLAN YEARS AFTER 2025; no substitution of its separate two-year introductory baseline or House March proposal. Both filing-compliance references retain HHS notification, advances for filer OR married spouse, the relevant tax-data year and failure to file/reconcile, with direct filer failure notice OR protected indirect risk/education notice; not a test imposed without those predicates or guaranteed notice-to-loss interval. ANY APPLICANT MAY use an Exchange-provided process BEGINNING NOT LATER THAN AUGUST 1 for the SUBSEQUENT PLAN YEAR; not a universal applicant deadline. Senate process covers HOUSEHOLD INCOME AND ENROLLMENT. Sections 112201/71303 apply to TAXABLE YEARS BEGINNING AFTER DECEMBER 31, 2027, distinct from the House discrepancy PLAN YEARS ON/AFTER JANUARY 1, 2026 and the Senate incorporated-rule duration. No automatic credit/coverage outcome, whole-package closure or component preference is inferred.

Senate cost-sharing dependency is now source-complete for this bounded question; no House annual filing/extension amendment or notice-version substitution is imported. NO reduction for ANY MONTH UNLESS a COVERAGE MONTH FOR WHICH 36B CREDIT IS ALLOWED TO THE INSURED OR AN APPLICABLE TAXPAYER ON THE INSURED'S BEHALF: necessary, not sufficient, and not every insured personally filing. Definitions share 36B terms; data use ADVANCE-DETERMINATION TAX YEAR, not credit-allowed tax year. The undeleted cost-sharing sentence/basic-health branch alone does not establish continuing benefits. Question 34 remains RESERVED, without actual credit/reduction/basic-health award or loss, legal repair, full-package closure or acceptance.

Senate tax is 1 percent and concerns only the named physical funding, subject to separate nonapplication alternatives. One alternative requires funds withdrawn from an account held in or by an institution described in (A)-(H); that institution must also be subject to BSA chapter 53/subchapter II. The other alternative requires funding with a US-issued debit or credit card. No any-bank/card exception or universal cash charge. WITHOUT REGARD TO debit (B) is not automatic exclusion of every prepaid card. No House citizen-verification/36C/6050BB mechanism is imported or a citizenship-based Senate exemption inferred. Both retain consumer/NATURAL-PERSON sender in a DEFINED STATE, provider-initiated ELECTRONIC transfer to FOREIGN designated recipient, account-independence, normal-course provider and SMALL-VALUE exclusion. Physical funding is distinct from electronic transfer technology. SENDER pays; provider COLLECTS FROM SENDER AND REMITS QUARTERLY; secondary liability ONLY unpaid-at-transfer AND uncollected extent. Transfers apply AFTER DECEMBER 31, 2025. Anti-conduit deeming/regulatory discretion is not observed avoidance, wrongdoing or an individual tax finding. No specific person, provider, transaction path, credit/refund or actual net-cost outcome is determined.

Selected Senate 71301/71302/71303 retain own eligible-alien/income/verification predicates and effective dates; these sections do not contain House named-memo amendments. No House title-wide/CSR-section/Federal-payment-sentence exclusion is imported, and no automatic DACA eligibility or whole-package absence of DACA effects is inferred. Original memo is historical context, not a current ACA eligibility decision.

The qualifying child's defined SSN is required in either case. The Senate also requires the taxpayer's defined SSN or, on a joint return, the defined SSN of at least one spouse. This is not both spouses on every joint return or a child number alone. No House SIMILAR 32(d) is imported. Own $2,200 context and after-2025 credit inflation; The senior mechanism in 70103 is addressed separately below. Both child-credit amendments begin with TAXABLE YEARS BEGINNING AFTER DECEMBER 31, 2024. The defined SSN may be issued to either a US citizen or an individual under the named work-authorized-alien branch. In either case, it must have been issued before the due date for the return. Any SSA number, an ITIN or citizenship proof alone is insufficient. Complete 24/152 retain own qualifying-child, NOT-ATTAINED-17, citizenship/residence/adoption, relationship/support/abode/joint-return/tie/custody and other exceptions, income/refundable/identification/year limits. Existing 24(h)(4)(C) PARAGRAPH (7) fallback is RETAINED but new claimant/spouse-failure application RESERVED as question 39: no guaranteed $500 or whole-family loss. Zero-exemption reference rule does not itself eliminate credit. Mathematical-error scope changes to SECTION 24; own alleged-error/explanation notice, no petition BASED ON THAT NOTICE, abatement request WITHIN 60 DAYS AFTER NOTICE SENT, mandatory abatement UPON RECEIPT, deficiency reassessment and collection stay remain. No actual fraud, debt, indexed payment, credit/refund, every-remedy loss or individual/tax-family determination.

The Senate $6,000 deduction is per qualified person. The listed alternatives are the taxpayer or the spouse on a joint return. In either case, the claimed person must have attained 65 before the tax year closes and must supply that person's defined SSN. One spouse's number does not establish deductions for both. The phaseout rate is 6 percent over $75,000, or $150,000 on a joint return. A taxpayer married within section 7703 must file jointly with the spouse; the new House similar-32(d) clause, blind bonus and hypothetical-itemizer mechanism are not imported. Own mathematical-error label is (W). The same-version SSN definition permits issuance to either a US citizen or the named work-authorized-alien category. In either case, the number must have been issued before the due date for the return. Other SSA numbers or ITINs do not alone qualify. Child-credit identification is not senior identification. Own taxable-income, itemization, spouse/exemption and marital predicates remain, along with the nonresident-alien standard-deduction exclusion, without an individual eligibility finding or accepted override. A deduction is not a dollar-for-dollar credit, exemption of all Social Security income or guaranteed refund. Both senior amendments apply to taxable years beginning after December 31, 2024; their own upper limit is a taxable year beginning before January 1, 2029. Modified income includes the named 911/931/933 exclusions. Mathematical-error notice requires the alleged error and explanation; the no-petition rule concerns that notice. The abatement request period is 60 days after notice is sent, abatement follows receipt, reassessment uses deficiency procedures and collection is stayed during the abatement period. No actual debt, fraud, payment or loss of every remedy.

Senate requires the individual's defined SSN in all cases. A credit for the qualified expenses of an individual other than the taxpayer or spouse must also include that individual's name and defined SSN. No new House spouse-number or similar-32(d) amendment is imported; retained 25A(g)(6) requires joint filing for a taxpayer married within 7703. No separate-return eligibility or child-credit joint-number alternative is inferred. The same-version defined SSN permits citizen issuance or the named work-authorized-alien branch. The AOTC student reference freezes HEA 484(a)(1), with its own exceptions, at August 5, 1997; it does not import all current student eligibility or its citizenship paragraph. The institution definition retains frozen HEA 481 and its own title IV eligibility condition. Exact historical passages and amendment chronology are bound; full HEA 481 comparison uses two declared split-word normalizations, without source mutation or personal/institution classification. A taxpayer nonresident during any portion of the year retains the conditional 6013(g)/(h) chapter-1 resident-election path, each with own spouse/status/both-election and duration/termination/re-election predicates; this is not all-noncitizen denial or immigration status/work authorization. Both apply to taxable years beginning after December 31, 2025. Own mathematical-error (J) changes TIN to SSN or EIN; alleged-error/explanation notice, 60 days after notice is sent, abatement upon receipt, deficiency reassessment and collection stay remain. No debt, wrongdoing, guaranteed credit/refund, loss of every remedy or whole-package closure.

Senate 100052 uses one additional fiscal year 2025 $29.85 billion ICE envelope through September 30, 2029 for listed purposes; no House account amounts or hiring minima imported. The Director may provide a retention bonus to a named ICE agent, officer or attorney who commits to two additional years of immigration-enforcement service. The Director may provide a signing bonus to a named ICE agent, officer or attorney only if that person is hired on or after enactment and commits to five years of immigration-enforcement service. No actual hiring/bonus/agreement/collection/removal/expenditure or full-package closure.

Senate 100054(2)/(3) drug/prosecution purposes use the shared $3.33 billion fiscal year 2025 envelope through September 30, 2029, without House earmarks. Own listed matters include unlawful voting; full 611 federal-office/exception/nonapplication predicates remain, no generic alien-guilt or new benefit/voting rule. Separate 100055 DOJ Fund. The Attorney General shall use the Fund amounts for grants to eligible States, State agencies, and units of local government, pursuant to their existing statutory authorities, for any of the following purposes. The paragraph 1 purpose is locating and apprehending aliens who have committed a crime under Federal, State, or local law, in addition to being unlawfully present in the United States. The paragraph 2 purpose is collection and analysis of law enforcement investigative information within the United States to counter gang or other criminal activity. The paragraph 3 purpose is investigating and prosecuting crimes committed by aliens within the United States and drug and human trafficking crimes committed within the United States. The paragraph 4 purpose is court operations related to the prosecution of crimes committed by aliens and drug and human trafficking crimes. The paragraph 5 purpose is temporary criminal detention of aliens. The paragraph 6 purpose is transporting aliens described in paragraph (1) within the United States to locations related to the apprehension, detention, and prosecution of such aliens. The paragraph 7 purpose is vehicle maintenance, logistics, transportation, and other support provided to law enforcement agencies by a State agency to enhance the ability to locate and apprehend aliens who have committed crimes under Federal, State, or local law, in addition to being unlawfully present in the United States. Paragraphs (1) and (7) retain their own additional-crime and unlawful-presence requirements; paragraph (6) retains the paragraph (1) person category, its domestic transport limit and its destination purposes. Those requirements are not imported into the other purposes. Temporary criminal detention is distinct from civil immigration detention. Court paragraph (4) prints no separate within-the-United-States phrase; no neighboring location condition is borrowed. Listed conjunctions report the source categories, not a determination that a particular grant must fund both crime categories. Existing statutory authorities do not create new State arrest/removal powers or establish actual crime/status/expense eligibility. Fiscal year 2025 appropriation is not to exceed $3,500,000,000 ($3.5 billion) until September 30, 2028, with qualified and documented expenses. The Attorney General may provide grants to State agencies and units of local government for their expenditures for completed, ongoing, or new activities determined to be eligible for such grant funding that occurred on or after January 20, 2021. Amounts made available under this section shall be distributed to more than 1 State. No borrowed January 21 or 2029 date, automatic grant, actual crime/status/detention/hiring/spending or full-package closure. Existing question 46 subsection-scope application is unchanged.

Senate 100051(9)/(10) use the additional fiscal year 2025 $2,055,000,000 DHS envelope through September 30, 2029, in accordance with 235(b)(1)/(c), without House earmarks, House's express 212(a)(2)/(3) grounds wording or regardless-of-presence phrase. Senate 100051(8) and (11) are purposes within the additional $2,055,000,000 fiscal year 2025 appropriation to the Secretary of Homeland Security, available through September 30, 2029. Neither purpose is a separate earmark for the full account, the ICE account or a House child appropriation. Paragraph (8) funds removal operations for specified unaccompanied alien children, but amounts under this paragraph shall only be used for permitting a specified unaccompanied alien child to withdraw the application for admission of the child pursuant to section 235(a)(4). The Secretary of Homeland Security must determine on a case-by-case basis all three specified-child conditions. First, the child has been found by an immigration officer at a land border or port of entry of the United States and is inadmissible under the Immigration and Nationality Act. Second, the child has not been a victim of severe forms of trafficking in persons, and there is no credible evidence that such child is at risk of being trafficked upon return of the child to the child's country of nationality or country of last habitual residence. Third, the child does not have a fear of returning to the child's country of nationality or country of last habitual residence owing to a credible fear of persecution. The paragraph does not print the House express contiguous-or-non-contiguous-country phrase or an independent-decision finding; neither is silently inserted into its definition. The incorporated unaccompanied-alien-child definition requires no lawful immigration status in the United States and not having attained 18 years of age, together with either no parent or legal guardian in the United States or no parent or legal guardian in the United States available to provide care and physical custody. The complete severe-forms-of-trafficking definition is bound with its own sex-trafficking and labor-or-services alternatives, force/fraud/coercion and under-18 distinctions; no label alone determines a child's eligibility. Paragraph (11) funds criminal and gang checks of defined unaccompanied alien children who are 12 years of age and older, including the examination of such unaccompanied alien children for gang-related tattoos and other gang-related markings. It prints no separate encountered-by-CBP condition; the House 70116 encounter condition is not imported. Its age-12 floor belongs to this check purpose, not the paragraph (8) withdrawal definition. Examination funding is not a finding that a child belongs to a gang, has committed a crime or is dangerous. Complete material captured pre-vote 235(a)(4) retains discretionary permission to withdraw and depart immediately, not a mandatory withdrawal or removal order. Complete TVPRA 235/1232 retains its own contiguous-child case-by-case trafficking/fear and independent-decision conditions, discretionary withdrawal/return, safe-return conditions, 48-hour screening and failed-or-undetermined-screen transfer, other-child custody pathway and own notification/72-hour-transfer exceptions. Its removal-proceedings, relief/access-to-counsel, placement, suitability and remaining safeguards retain their own scope. Senate funding does not itself establish their repeal, fulfillment or a universal individual return, protection or counsel outcome. Exact application interaction remains separate question 49; House question 43 is preserved independently.

Senate 100051(5) fingerprint and DNA purposes are within the additional $2,055,000,000 fiscal year 2025 Secretary of Homeland Security account through September 30, 2029. Both purposes share the printed circumstance of aliens and alien children entering the United States without a valid visa. Subparagraph (A) funds collecting fingerprints, in accordance with section 262 and subsections (a)(3) and (b) of section 235 of the Immigration and Nationality Act. Subparagraph (B) separately funds collecting DNA, in accordance with sections 235(d) and 287(b) of that Act. These are funding purposes with their own incorporated authorities, not a determination that every alien or child is subject to every collection power or that funded collection actually occurred. Captured 262(a) concerns an alien now or hereafter in the United States who is fourteen years of age or older, has not been registered and fingerprinted under section 1201(b) or section 30 or 31 of the Alien Registration Act, 1940, and remains in the United States for thirty days or longer. All those conditions are common to its duty to apply for registration and to be fingerprinted before the expiration of such thirty days. Captured 262(b) separately requires a parent or legal guardian to apply for registration of an alien now or hereafter in the United States who is less than fourteen years of age, has not been registered under those named provisions, and remains in the United States for thirty days or longer, before that period expires. That parent/guardian provision prints registration, not the same under-14 fingerprint duty. Whenever an alien attains his fourteenth birthday in the United States, the separate rule requires in-person registration and fingerprinting within thirty days thereafter. Captured 262(c) retains the Attorney General's discretionary nonimmigrant fingerprint waiver on the basis of reciprocity pursuant to prescribed regulations; no actual waiver is inferred. Complete 235(a)(3) concerns inspection of aliens, including crewmen, who apply for or otherwise seek admission, readmission or transit; it does not itself print a fingerprint command. Complete material 235(b)(1)/(2) screening, exceptions, asylum/fear/interview/review/consultation/detention and contiguous-return conditions remain bound, together with the original favorable-admission challenge. January 29, 2025 Public Law 119-1 renumbers that original challenge from (3) to (4) and inserts the distinct State enforcement (3); the captured 2024 wording is not relabeled as an unamended 2025 subsection. Complete 235(d) retains its own belief-based conveyance search, detention/delivery with the alien-crewmember exception, named oath/evidence powers and subpoena-purpose/court-enforcement conditions. Complete 287(b) retains the designated officer/employee oath/evidence scope and its own knowing-or-willful false-evidence/perjury conditions. Neither cited provision expressly names DNA collection. That literal observation does not resolve whether other law, implementation rules or this funding language supports a proposed collection; question 50 reserves the exact DNA authority/application interaction. Question 51 separately reserves the fingerprint-purpose no-valid-visa circumstance alongside the incorporated registration age/prior-registration/duration/waiver paths and inspection procedures. No statutory repeal, guaranteed discretion outcome, universal biometric collection or actual child/parent/status/registration finding is inferred.

Remaining Senate 100051 purposes (1) through (4), (6), (7) and (12) share the additional $2,055,000,000 fiscal year 2025 appropriation to the Secretary of Homeland Security, available through September 30, 2029. They are purposes within that account, not separate full-envelope earmarks or borrowed ICE/House amounts. The paragraph 1 purpose is hiring and training of additional U.S. Customs and Border Protection agents, and the necessary support staff, to carry out immigration enforcement activities. The paragraph 2 purpose is funding for transportation costs and related costs associated with the departure or removal of aliens. The paragraph 3 purpose is funding for the assignment of Department of Homeland Security employees and State officers to carry out immigration enforcement activities pursuant to sections 103(a) and 287(g) of the Immigration and Nationality Act (8 U.S.C. 1103(a) and 1357(g)). The paragraph 4 purpose is hiring additional staff and investing the necessary resources to enhance screening and vetting of all aliens seeking entry into United States, consistent with section 212 of such Act (8 U.S.C. 1182), or intending to remain in the United States, consistent with section 237 of such Act (8 U.S.C. 1227). The paragraph 6 purpose is transporting and facilitating the return, pursuant to section 235(b)(2)(C) of the Immigration and Nationality Act (8 U.S.C. 1225(b)(2)(C)), of aliens arriving from contiguous territory. The paragraph 7 purpose is funding for State and local participation in homeland security efforts for purposes of: ending the presence of criminal gangs and criminal organizations throughout the United States; addressing crime and public safety threats; combating human smuggling and trafficking networks throughout the United States; supporting immigration enforcement activities; and providing reimbursement for State and local participation in such efforts. The paragraph 12 purpose is information technology investments to support immigration purposes, including improvements to fee and revenue collections. The entry and intended-remain screening categories retain their own section 212 and section 237 references. The State/local participation list retains all five own purposes, including its own throughout-the-United-States phrases. It does not borrow the reimbursement fund's crime-plus-unlawful-presence category or domestic transport restriction. The general departure/removal transportation purpose prints no separate within-the-United-States phrase. The assignment list retains Department of Homeland Security employees and State officers pursuant to both printed statutory references, not authority for any State employee to exercise all Federal powers. The printed purpose lists do not determine that a particular expenditure must fulfill every listed category. Fee and revenue collection IT is not a new fee, fine or penalty charge. Complete captured 103(a) retains its named agency roles, regulatory/delegation powers, consents and other conditions. In captured 103(a)(10), the Attorney General may authorize a State or local law enforcement officer to perform or exercise any of the powers, privileges, or duties conferred or imposed by this chapter or regulations issued thereunder upon officers or employees of the Service only in the event of the Attorney General's determination that an actual or imminent mass influx of aliens arriving off the coast of the United States, or near a land border, presents urgent circumstances requiring an immediate Federal response, and with the consent of the head of the department, agency, or establishment under whose jurisdiction the individual is serving. The captured event-specific authorization does not establish general unconditioned State power. Previously bound full 287(g) agreement qualifications, training, written powers/duration, Federal direction/supervision, voluntary/communication/cooperation and expense/employment/liability distinctions remain unchanged. Complete captured section 212(a) grounds and remaining operative section 212 authorities retain their own standards, exceptions, discretionary waivers and conditional notice rules, not an every-alien crime finding or guaranteed notice/waiver. January 29, 2025 Public Law 119-1 replaces the original Attorney General references in 212(d)(5) with Secretary of Homeland Security and adds the distinct State enforcement route. Original captured 2024 words are preserved with that amending law, not relabeled as the complete unamended 2025 section. Complete captured section 237 retains distinct deportability grounds, actual conviction/knowledge/timing or other own requirements, exceptions/waivers, special nonimmigrant and SIJ boundaries and conditional administrative stays; screening funding does not determine an individual inadmissible, deportable or criminal. The contiguous-return purpose is pursuant to 235(b)(2)(C). The captured 235(b)(2)(C) return authority concerns an applicant for admission whom the examining immigration officer determines is not clearly and beyond a doubt entitled to be admitted, arriving on land (whether or not at a designated port of arrival) from a foreign territory contiguous to the United States. The Attorney General may return that alien to that territory pending a proceeding under section 1229a. The captured parent exceptions for a crewman, an alien to whom paragraph (1) applies, and a stowaway remain. Discretionary return is not a final removal order or universal cross-border return duty. Complete captured 240 proceedings retain judge/charge/exclusive-procedure exceptions, own representation and evidence/examination limits, burdens, decision/appeal, motion and notice/deadline/stay rules. No guaranteed relief, government-paid counsel or individual hearing/return result is inferred. Other H.R.1 immigration components and separately reserved application questions remain unfinished.

The Senate 90005(b) State Border Security Reinforcement Fund is a distinct DHS fund. Its complete selected operative clauses are retained below. Senate 90005(b) paragraph 1: There is established, in the Department of Homeland Security, a fund to be known as the ``State Border Security Reinforcement Fund.'' Senate 90005(b) paragraph 2: The Secretary of Homeland Security shall use amounts appropriated or otherwise made available for the Fund for grants to eligible States and units of local government for any of the following purposes: Senate 90005(b) purpose A: Construction or installation of a border wall, border fencing or other barrier, or buoys along the southern border of the United States, which may include planning, procurement of materials, and personnel costs related to such construction or installation. Senate 90005(b) purpose B: Any work necessary to prepare the ground at or near land borders to allow construction and maintenance of a border wall or other barrier fencing. Senate 90005(b) purpose C: Detection and interdiction of illicit substances and aliens who have unlawfully entered the United States and have committed a crime under Federal, State, or local law, and transfer or referral of such aliens to the Department of Homeland Security as provided by law. Senate 90005(b) purpose D: Relocation of aliens who are unlawfully present in the United States from small population centers to other domestic locations. Senate 90005(b) paragraph 3: In addition to amounts otherwise available for the purposes described in paragraph (2), there is appropriated for fiscal year 2025, out of any money in the Treasury not otherwise appropriated, to the Department of Homeland Security for the State Border Security Reinforcement Fund established by paragraph (1), $10,000,000,000, to remain available until September 30, 2034, for qualified expenses for such purposes. Senate 90005(b) paragraph 4: The Secretary of Homeland Security may provide grants from the fund established by paragraph (1) to State agencies and units of local governments for expenditures made for completed, ongoing, or new activities, in accordance with law, that occurred on or after January 20, 2021. Senate 90005(b) paragraph 5: Each State desiring to apply for a grant under this subsection shall submit an application to the Secretary containing such information in support of the application as the Secretary may require. The Secretary shall require that each State include in its application the purposes for which the State seeks the funds and a description of how the State plans to allocate the funds. The Secretary shall begin to accept applications not later than 90 days after the date of the enactment of this Act. Senate 90005(b) paragraph 6: Nothing in this subsection shall authorize any State or local government to exercise immigration or border security authorities reserved exclusively to the Federal Government under the Immigration and Nationality Act (8 U.S.C. 1101 et seq.) or the Homeland Security Act of 2002 (6 U.S.C. 101 et seq.). The Federal Emergency Management Agency may use not more than 1 percent of the funds made available under this subsection for the purpose of administering grants provided for in this section. The paragraph (2)(C) alien category retains both unlawful entry and commission of a crime under Federal, State, or local law; those alien predicates do not classify illicit substances. Transfer or referral remains as provided by law. Paragraph (2)(D) instead concerns unlawful presence and relocation from small population centers to other domestic locations; it does not borrow the crime or unlawful-entry predicates from (C), or authorize an international return. Only (A) specifies the southern border; (B) says at or near land borders. The paragraph (2) eligible-State/local-unit grant purpose rule and paragraph (4) discretionary State-agency/local-government expenditure rule remain distinct. The paragraph (5) application obligations name each State; no additional local-government obligation is inferred. The 90-day clause concerns when the Secretary must begin accepting applications, not an applicant deadline or a finding that applications are open. The paragraph (6) construction rule preserves exclusively Federal authorities without deciding which actual functions or expenditures fall within that reservation. The FEMA administration ceiling is discretionary, no more than 1 percent of funds under this subsection for grants in this section; its two scope words remain distinct. This is not an actual award, expenditure, eligibility, individual status/crime, relocation, power delegation or reimbursement determination. House reimbursement amounts, availability, January 21 date and duplicate-reimbursement restriction are not imported. Other package components and the 51 separately reserved application questions remain unfinished.

Selected Senate 90005(a) funding and its own program context follow. Senate 90005(a) paragraph 1: In addition to amounts otherwise available, there is appropriated to the Administrator of the Federal Emergency Management Agency for fiscal year 2025, out of any money in the Treasury not otherwise appropriated, to remain available until September 30, 2029, to be administered under the State Homeland Security Grant Program authorized under section 2004 of the Homeland Security Act of 2002 (6 U.S.C. 605), to enhance State, local, and Tribal security through grants, contracts, cooperative agreements, and other activities-- Senate 90005(a) purpose A: $500,000,000 for State and local capabilities to detect, identify, track, or monitor threats from unmanned aircraft systems (as such term is defined in section 44801 of title 49, United States Code), consistent with titles 18 and 49 of the United States Code; Senate 90005(a) purpose B: $625,000,000 for security and other costs related to the 2026 FIFA World Cup; Senate 90005(a) purpose C: $1,000,000,000 for security, planning, and other costs related to the 2028 Olympics; and Senate 90005(a) purpose D: $450,000,000 for the Operation Stonegarden Grant Program. Senate 90005(a) paragraph 2: None of the funds made available under subparagraph (B) or (C) of paragraph (1) shall be subject to the requirements of section 2004(e)(1) or section 2008(a)(12) of the Homeland Security Act of 2002 (6 U.S.C. 605(e)(1), 609(a)(12)). The pre-vote fiscal year 2024 DHS/FEMA HSGP notice reproduced on Hawaii's official host describes Operation Stonegarden as supporting enhanced cooperation and coordination among CBP, USBP, and Federal, State, local, Tribal and territorial law enforcement agencies to improve overall border security. It funds joint border-security efforts along routes of ingress and egress to and from international borders, including travel corridors in States bordering Mexico and Canada and States and territories with international water borders. In that notice, those State, local, Tribal and territorial law enforcement agencies use their inherent law enforcement authorities and receive no additional authority from participating in Stonegarden. This is dated program-purpose context, not a new power conferred by the Senate appropriation or a complete 2025 eligibility rule. The additional fiscal year 2025 appropriation names FEMA Administrator, availability until September 30, 2029, administration under the State Homeland Security Grant Program in 6 U.S.C. 605, and State/local/Tribal security through grants, contracts, cooperative agreements and other activities. The Stonegarden purpose is $450,000,000 within that administration provision. The drone-threat, FIFA and Olympics purposes retain their own printed objects and amounts as adjacent context; those purposes alone do not establish an immigration purpose. The exemption from 605(e)(1) minimum allocation and 609(a)(12) grant-administration expense cap expressly names only FIFA paragraph (1)(B) and Olympics paragraph (1)(C); no exemption for Stonegarden paragraph (1)(D) or drone paragraph (1)(A) is inferred. Captured 605(e)(1) retains its State and named-territory minimum-allocation branches, own fiscal-year denominators and percentages; captured 609(a)(12) permits expenses directly related to grant administration except that such expenses may not exceed 3 percent of the grant amount. Neither this cap nor those minima are reclassified as the separate 90005(b) FEMA one-percent ceiling. Complete captured 603, 605 and 609 retain their own program relationships, application/distribution/multistate rules, permitted-use and personnel/construction/recreation restrictions, waivers, reimbursement, transfers and equipment requirements. Their application to a particular 2025 Stonegarden award, including interaction with the dated 2024 notice's separate HSGP components and conditions, is reserved as question 52. No 2024 funding amount, application deadline, performance period, subrecipient tier or approval automatically governs this new appropriation. No particular State/local/Tribal award, entitlement, expenditure, additional law-enforcement power or individual status result is inferred. Other package components and all previously reserved application questions remain unfinished.

Selected exact Senate 70119 death/disability loan-discharge income-exclusion and SSN provisions follow. Senate 70119 exclusion grounds: In the case of an individual, gross income does not include any amount which (but for this subsection) would be includible in gross income for such taxable year by reason of the discharge (in whole or in part) of any loan described in subparagraph (B), if such discharge was-- (i) pursuant to subsection (a) or (d) of section 437 of the Higher Education Act of 1965 or the parallel benefit under part D of title IV of such Act (relating to the repayment of loan liability), (ii) pursuant to section 464(c)(1)(F) of such Act, or (iii) otherwise discharged on account of death or total and permanent disability of the student. Senate 70119 loan categories: A loan is described in this subparagraph if such loan is-- (i) a student loan (as defined in paragraph (2)), or (ii) a private education loan (as defined in section 140(a) of the Consumer Credit Protection Act (15 U.S.C. 1650(a)). Senate 70119 identification and own marital rules: (i) In general.--Subparagraph (A) shall not apply with respect to any discharge during any taxable year unless the taxpayer includes the taxpayer's social security number on the return of tax for such taxable year. (ii) Social security number.--For purposes of this subparagraph, the term `social security number' has the meaning given such term in section 24(h)(7).. Senate 70119 math-error amendment: Section 6213(g)(2), as amended by this Act, is further amended by striking and at the end of subparagraph (V), by striking the period at the end of subparagraph (W) and inserting , and, and by inserting after subparagraph (W) the following new subparagraph: (X) an omission of a correct social security number required under section 108(f)(5)(C) (relating to discharges on account of death or disability).. Senate 70119 discharge-date applicability: The amendments made by this section shall apply to discharges after December 31, 2025. Each version replaces only 108(f)(5) with the printed exclusion, not all of section 108 or every student-loan tax rule. The original 2024 (5) instead covers its defined discharge categories after December 31, 2020 and before January 1, 2026; the candidate does not silently extend that entire temporary rule unchanged. The common requirement that the discharged loan meet new subparagraph (B) applies across all three ground alternatives. Interaction of that gate, complete loan definitions and the parent-borrower 437(d) reference is reserved as question 55; no blanket conclusion that every HEA discharge qualifies for tax exclusion. Original (f)(1) service-conditioned discharge and (4) named repayment-program exclusions remain separate. New loan categories retain full 108(f)(2) student-loan definition and entire 140(a) private-education definitions, including actual (a)(8) private loan, own private-lender and expense meanings and excluded credit/mortgage categories. This does not mean every education-related debt qualifies. The three exclusion-ground alternatives remain separate: the first two use their specified HEA discharge paths, while only the third prints otherwise discharged on account of death or total and permanent disability of the student. A parent borrower is not silently equated to the student. Full 437(a) retains qualifying loans, death/disability determinations, safeguards, conditional reinstatement, VA documentation and own income-monitoring/approval/opt-out/update rules; 437(d) separately addresses a parent loan when the student dies. Captured 464(c)(1)(F) retains loan-fund agreement scope, borrower death, regulated permanent/total disability, the medically determinable substantial-gainful-activity alternative with its own duration/death tests, and VA unemployability due to service-connected disability. Part D parallel benefit is retained with complete captured 455 and its unless-otherwise-specified limitation, not a universal cancellation promise. Tax exclusion after a qualifying discharge is distinct from authority to cancel a loan. Selected exact Senate account and separate pilot eligibility clauses follow. Senate 70204 IRA treatment with own exceptions: Except as provided in this section or under regulations or guidance established by the Secretary, a Trump account shall be treated for purposes of this title in the same manner as an individual retirement account under section 408(a). Senate 70204 account establishment and instrument: The term `Trump account' means an individual retirement account (as defined in section 408(a)) which is not designated as a Roth IRA and which meets the following requirements: (A) The account-- (i) is created or organized by the Secretary for the exclusive benefit of an eligible individual or such eligible individual's beneficiaries, or (ii) is-- (I) created or organized in the United States for the exclusive benefit of an individual who has not attained the age of 18 before the end of the calendar year, or such individual's beneficiaries, and (II) funded by a qualified rollover contribution. (B) The account is designated (in such manner as the Secretary shall prescribe) at the time of the establishment of the account as a Trump account. (C) The written governing instrument creating the account meets the following requirements: (i) No contribution will be accepted-- (I) before the date that is 12 months after the date of the enactment of this section, or (II) in the case of a contribution made in any calendar year before the calendar year in which the account beneficiary attains age 18, if such contribution would result in aggregate contributions (other than exempt contributions) for such calendar year in excess of the contribution limit specified in subsection (c)(2)(A). (ii) Except as provided in subsection (d), no distribution will be allowed before the first day of the calendar year in which the account beneficiary attains age 18. (iii) No part of the account funds will be invested in any asset other than an eligible investment during any period before the first day of the calendar year in which the account beneficiary attains age 18. Senate 70204 eligible individual and reciprocal election paths: The term `eligible individual' means any individual-- (A) who has not attained the age of 18 before the close of the calendar year in which the election under subparagraph (C) is made, (B) for whom a social security number (within the meaning of section 24(h)(7)) has been issued before the date on which an election under subsection (C) is made, and (C) for whom-- (i) an election is made under this subparagraph by the Secretary if the Secretary determines (based on information available to the Secretary from tax returns or otherwise) that such individual meets the requirements of subparagraphs (A) and (B) and no prior election has been made for such individual under clause (ii), or (ii) an election is made under this subparagraph by a person other than the Secretary (at such time and in such manner as the Secretary may prescribe) for the establishment of a Trump account if no prior election has been made for such individual under clause (i). Senate 70204 account beneficiary: The term `account beneficiary' means the individual on whose behalf the Trump account was established. Senate 70204 full-balance account rollover: For purposes of this section, the term `qualified rollover contribution' means an amount which is paid in a direct trustee-to-trustee transfer from a Trump account maintained for the benefit of the account beneficiary to a Trump account maintained for such beneficiary, but only if the amount of such payment is equal to the entire balance of the Trump account from which the payment is made. Senate 70204 elected child payment: In the case of an individual who makes an election under this section with respect to an eligible child of the individual, such eligible child shall be treated as making a payment against the tax imposed by subtitle A (for the taxable year for which the election was made) in an amount equal to $1,000. Senate 70204 refund to child account: The amount treated as a payment under subsection (a) shall be paid by the Secretary to the Trump account with respect to which such eligible child is the account beneficiary. Senate 70204 pilot birth window, no prior election and citizenship: For purposes of this section, the term `eligible child' means a qualifying child (as defined in section 152(c))-- (1) who is born after December 31, 2024, and before January 1, 2029, (2) with respect to whom no prior election has been made under this section by such individual or any other individual, and (3) who is a United States citizen. Senate 70204 pilot child identification and election-date definition: (1) In general.--This section shall not apply to any taxpayer unless such individual includes with the election made under this section the social security number of the eligible child with respect to whom the election is made. (2) Social security number defined.--For purposes of paragraph (1), the term `social security number' shall have the meaning given such term in section 24(h)(7), determined by substituting `before the date of the election made under section 6434' for `before the due date of such return' in subparagraph (B) thereof. Senate 70204 payment offset exception: Any payment made to any individual under this section shall not be-- (1) subject to reduction or offset pursuant to subsection (c), (d), (e), or (f) of section 6402 or any similar authority permitting offset, or (2) reduced or offset by other assessed Federal taxes that would otherwise be subject to levy or collection.
